bone biology.md:
## 1. Composition of bone
- **By weight:** about **60-70% inorganic mineral**, **20-25% organic matrix**, about **5-10% water**; cells form a very small fraction. (By dry weight: about 60% inorganic, 40% organic.)
- **Bone stores about 99% of body calcium** and about **85% of phosphate**.

### Organic matrix (osteoid)
- **Type I collagen = about 90% of the organic matrix**.
  - Triple helix of **two alpha-1 chains and one alpha-2 chain** (COL1A1, COL1A2), **glycine at every third residue** (Gly-X-Y; X and Y often proline and hydroxyproline).
  - **Hydroxylation of proline and lysine needs vitamin C** (scurvy) and iron; **cross-links** (pyridinoline, deoxypyridinoline) give tensile strength; their breakdown products are **resorption markers**.
  - Collagen fibrils are arranged with **"hole zones" (gaps) between molecules** where mineral is first deposited.
  - Gives bone its **tensile strength**; mineral gives **compressive strength** and stiffness.
- **Non-collagenous proteins (about 10%)**:

| Protein | Made by | Role / exam point |
|---|---|---|
| **Osteocalcin** (bone gla protein) | **Osteoblasts** | **Most abundant non-collagenous protein**; **vitamin K-dependent** gamma-carboxylation; **stimulated by 1,25(OH)2D**; attracts osteoclasts, regulates mineralisation; **serum marker of bone formation**; acts as a hormone on insulin secretion |
| **Osteonectin** (SPARC) | Osteoblasts, platelets | Binds **calcium and collagen**, regulates mineralisation |
| **Osteopontin**, bone sialoprotein | Osteoblasts | **Cell attachment** proteins (RGD sequences) that **anchor osteoclasts** via integrins |
| **Proteoglycans** (decorin, biglycan) | | Regulate collagen fibril diameter and mineralisation |
| **Growth factors** (BMPs, TGF-beta, IGF, PDGF, FGF) | Stored in matrix | Released during resorption (coupling) |
| Alkaline phosphatase | **Osteoblasts** (membrane-bound) | Hydrolyses **pyrophosphate (a mineralisation inhibitor)**; **bone-specific ALP is a formation marker**; low in hypophosphatasia |

### Inorganic matrix
- **Calcium hydroxyapatite: Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2**, as small plate-like crystals; also **amorphous calcium phosphate** and **osteocalcium phosphate (brushite)**.
- **Fluoride** substitutes for hydroxyl (fluorapatite: harder but brittle bone; fluorosis).
- **Mineralisation:** **matrix vesicles** from osteoblasts and hypertrophic chondrocytes concentrate calcium and phosphate; **ALP removes pyrophosphate**; crystals nucleate in collagen hole zones. **Mineralisation lag time** about **10-15 days**; widened osteoid seams = osteomalacia.

## 2. Bone cells
### Osteoblasts (bone-forming)
- **Origin:** **mesenchymal stem cells** (bone marrow stroma, periosteum).
- **Key transcription factors:** **RUNX2 (CBFA1)** (master switch; mutation causes **cleidocranial dysplasia**) and **osterix (SP7)** downstream of RUNX2. Adipocyte differentiation needs PPAR-gamma; chondrocyte, **SOX9**.
- **Wnt/beta-catenin pathway** drives osteoblast formation:
  - Wnt binds **Frizzled with the co-receptor LRP5/6**, stabilising beta-catenin.
  - **LRP5 loss-of-function: osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome**; **LRP5 gain-of-function: high bone mass**.
  - **Inhibitors:** **sclerostin** (SOST gene, from **osteocytes**; loss causes **sclerosteosis** and **van Buchem disease**), **DKK1** (Dickkopf-1; raised in **myeloma**, causing purely lytic lesions without blastic response).
  - **Romosozumab** = anti-sclerostin antibody (anabolic and antiresorptive).
- **Products:** **type I collagen**, osteocalcin, ALP, bone sialoprotein, **RANKL and OPG** (osteoblasts control osteoclasts).
- **Receptors:** **PTH/PTHrP receptor (PTH1R)**, **1,25(OH)2D**, **oestrogen**, glucocorticoids, prostaglandins, growth factors. **Osteoclasts lack PTH receptors**: PTH stimulates resorption **indirectly** via osteoblast RANKL.
- **Intermittent PTH** (teriparatide, abaloparatide) is **anabolic** (increased osteoblast number and survival); **continuous** high PTH is **catabolic**.
- **Fates:** become **osteocytes** (about 10-20%), **lining cells**, or undergo **apoptosis** (most).

### Osteocytes
- **Most numerous bone cells: about 90-95% of cells** in mature bone; former osteoblasts trapped in **lacunae**, connected by **dendritic processes in canaliculi** (gap junctions, connexin 43).
- **Mechanosensors:** detect **fluid shear stress** in the lacuno-canalicular network and orchestrate remodelling (**Wolff's law** at the cellular level).
- **Products:** **sclerostin** (inhibits bone formation; **reduced by loading**, increased by unloading), **RANKL** (main source for remodelling), **FGF23** (phosphaturic hormone).
- **Osteocyte apoptosis** (steroids, unloading, microdamage) triggers targeted remodelling.
- Regulate **phosphate** via FGF23, PHEX and DMP1 (mutations cause hypophosphataemic rickets).

### Osteoclasts (bone-resorbing)
- **Origin: haematopoietic monocyte-macrophage lineage** (not mesenchymal): explains why **stem-cell transplant cures infantile osteopetrosis**.
- **Essential factors:** **M-CSF** (macrophage colony-stimulating factor) and **RANKL** (binds RANK on precursors, NF-kappa-B signalling); fuse into **multinucleated cells** (usually up to about 10 nuclei).
- **Structure and mechanism:**
  - **Sealing zone:** **alpha-v-beta-3 integrin** binds RGD sequences of osteopontin and bone sialoprotein, isolating a resorption compartment.
  - **Ruffled border:** increases surface area; **H+ ATPase proton pump** acidifies the compartment (dissolves mineral); **chloride channel (CLCN7)**; **carbonic anhydrase II** supplies H+.
  - **Cathepsin K** (lysosomal cysteine protease) digests collagen; **matrix metalloproteinases** help.
  - Resorption pits = **Howship lacunae**.
  - **TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase)** is the histochemical marker; **calcitonin receptor** present (calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts **directly**).
- **Defects:**

| Defect | Disease |
|---|---|
| Carbonic anhydrase II | **Osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis** and cerebral calcification |
| Proton pump (TCIRG1) or chloride channel (CLCN7) | **Osteopetrosis** (malignant infantile; CLCN7 also adult benign form) |
| **Cathepsin K** | **Pyknodysostosis** |
| RANKL / RANK loss | Osteoclast-poor osteopetrosis |
| RANK activating / SQSTM1 | Familial expansile osteolysis / **Paget disease** |

### RANKL-RANK-OPG system (coupling of formation and resorption)
- **RANKL** (from osteoblasts, osteocytes, activated T cells, synovial cells) binds **RANK** on osteoclast precursors: osteoclast formation, activation, survival.
- **Osteoprotegerin (OPG)**: a **soluble decoy receptor** for RANKL made by osteoblasts; blocks osteoclastogenesis.
- **RANKL:OPG ratio** sets resorption. **Increased** by PTH, 1,25(OH)2D, glucocorticoids, IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, prostaglandins, **oestrogen deficiency**; **decreased (OPG up)** by oestrogen.
- **Denosumab** is a monoclonal antibody against **RANKL** (mimics OPG); rebound vertebral fractures when stopped without follow-on therapy.
- **Clinical:** RANKL drives osteolysis in **giant cell tumour of bone** (stromal cells express RANKL; **denosumab** used), **myeloma, lytic metastases**, **rheumatoid erosions**, **periprosthetic osteolysis** (wear particles activate macrophages: TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, RANKL).

### Bisphosphonate mechanism (frequently examined)
- **Pyrophosphate analogues** (P-C-P backbone) that bind hydroxyapatite and are taken up by osteoclasts during resorption.
- **Nitrogen-containing** (alendronate, risedronate, ibandronate, pamidronate, **zoledronate**, most potent): inhibit **farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase** in the **mevalonate (HMG-CoA reductase) pathway**, preventing prenylation of small GTPases (Ras, Rho, Rab) needed for the ruffled border: osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis.
- **Non-nitrogen** (etidronate, clodronate, tiludronate): metabolised into **toxic ATP analogues** that cause osteoclast apoptosis; etidronate impairs mineralisation.

## 3. Types and structure of bone
### Woven vs lamellar
| Feature | **Woven (immature)** | **Lamellar (mature)** |
|---|---|---|
| Collagen | **Random**, coarse | **Organised, stress-oriented** layers |
| Mechanics | **Isotropic**, weak, flexible | **Anisotropic**, strong |
| Turnover / cells | Rapid formation, many cells | Slower, fewer cells |
| Where normal | **Embryonic skeleton, physeal metaphysis, fracture callus** | Normal adult bone |
| Where pathological | **Paget, fibrous dysplasia, osteosarcoma, hyperparathyroidism, OI**, myositis ossificans (early) | |

### Cortical vs cancellous
| Feature | **Cortical (compact)** | **Cancellous (trabecular)** |
|---|---|---|
| Share of skeletal mass | **About 80%** | About 20% |
| Porosity | Low (about 10%) | High (50-90%) |
| Surface area | Small | **Large** (most metabolic activity) |
| **Turnover** | Slow | **Much faster** (several times) |
| Stiffness (Young's modulus) | **High** | Lower |
| Structural unit | **Osteon (Haversian system)** | Trabeculae (packets) |
| First lost in | Hyperparathyroidism, ageing (cortical thinning, porosity) | **Postmenopausal osteoporosis**, steroids |

- **Osteon (Haversian system):** concentric lamellae around a central **Haversian canal** (vessels, nerves), running along the long axis; **Volkmann canals** connect them transversely; **cement lines** mark the osteon boundary (weak point; cracks stop there).
- **Interstitial lamellae** fill spaces between osteons; **circumferential lamellae** line the inner and outer surfaces.
- **Periosteum:** outer **fibrous layer** (Sharpey fibres anchor tendons and ligaments) and inner **cambium (osteogenic) layer**; **thick and osteogenic in children** (rapid callus, remodelling).
- **Endosteum:** lines the medullary canal.

## 4. Blood supply of long bones
- **Bone receives about 10% of cardiac output** (traditional figure; quoted around 5-10%).
- **Three systems:**
  1. **Nutrient artery** (high-pressure): enters the diaphysis through the nutrient foramen, divides into ascending and descending branches; supplies the **inner two-thirds of the cortex** (endosteal supply).
  2. **Metaphyseal-epiphyseal arteries**: from periarticular plexuses (e.g. geniculate arteries); anastomose with the nutrient system after physeal closure.
  3. **Periosteal vessels** (low-pressure): supply the **outer one-third of the cortex**; important in children and after fracture.
- **Flow is centrifugal** (endosteal to periosteal, inside-out) in normal mature bone because the nutrient system is high pressure.
- **After a displaced fracture or reaming**, the endosteal supply is disrupted and **flow becomes centripetal** (periosteal supply dominates). **Reaming** destroys the endosteal supply temporarily (it regenerates within weeks) and increases periosteal flow; **stripping the periosteum** (plating) adds to devascularisation: basis of **biological (bridge, minimally invasive) fixation**.
- **Venous drainage**: central venous sinus.
- **Fracture healing raises blood flow** (peaks about 2 weeks).

## 5. Bone formation (ossification)
| Type | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Endochondral** | **Cartilage model** replaced by bone | **Long bones**, physeal growth, **fracture callus (secondary healing)**, embryonic axial and appendicular skeleton |
| **Intramembranous** | **Direct** from mesenchymal condensations, **no cartilage stage** | **Flat bones of the skull, maxilla, mandible**, most of the **clavicle**, **distraction osteogenesis**, rigid (primary) fracture healing in the cutting-cone sense |
| **Appositional** | Osteoblasts lay bone on existing surfaces | **Periosteal growth in width**, bone remodelling |

- **Distraction osteogenesis** (Ilizarov) forms bone by **intramembranous ossification** at about **1 mm per day** (0.25 mm four times a day), after a **latency** of about 5-7 days; low-energy **corticotomy** preserving periosteum and medullary blood supply.
- **Embryology:** limb buds appear at about **4 weeks**; **primary ossification centres** in long bones appear by about **7-8 weeks** (the **clavicle is first, at about 5-6 weeks**, intramembranous); secondary centres mostly after birth (the **distal femur at about 36-40 weeks** is present at birth: a sign of fetal maturity).
- **Endochondral sequence:** mesenchymal condensation, chondrocyte differentiation (SOX9), hypertrophy (**type X collagen**, VEGF), vascular invasion, osteoblasts lay bone on calcified cartilage (**primary spongiosa**), remodelled to secondary spongiosa.

## 6. The physis (growth plate)
### Zones (epiphysis to metaphysis)
| Zone | Features | Associated disorders |
|---|---|---|
| **Reserve (resting, germinal)** | Few scattered cells, **matrix production and storage** (lipids, glycogen, proteoglycans); **low oxygen tension** | **Gaucher disease**; **diastrophic dysplasia**, **pseudoachondroplasia** and **Kniest dysplasia** (defective matrix proteins/processing) |
| **Proliferative** | Cells **stack in columns**, divide; **longitudinal growth**; high oxygen and proteoglycan inhibiting mineralisation | **Achondroplasia (FGFR3)**, gigantism (GH excess), hereditary multiple exostoses (EXT), malnutrition, irradiation |
| **Hypertrophic** (maturation, degeneration, **provisional calcification**) | Chondrocytes **enlarge 5-10 times**, accumulate calcium, **type X collagen**, matrix calcifies, chondrocyte **apoptosis**; low oxygen | **Rickets** (widened zone of provisional calcification fails to mineralise), **SCFE** (hypertrophic zone), **Salter-Harris fractures** (through the zone of provisional calcification, the weakest), enchondroma, **mucopolysaccharidoses**, **Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (COL10A1)** |
| **Metaphysis: primary spongiosa** | Vascular invasion, osteoblasts lay woven bone on calcified cartilage bars | **Scurvy**, **acute haematogenous osteomyelitis** (sluggish flow in sinusoidal loops), metaphyseal chondrodysplasias |
| **Metaphysis: secondary spongiosa** | Remodelling to lamellar bone | **Osteopetrosis** (failure of remodelling), osteogenesis imperfecta, **Erlenmeyer flask** (Gaucher, osteopetrosis) |

- **Physeal fractures** usually pass through the **zone of provisional calcification of the hypertrophic zone**; the germinal/proliferative zones stay with the epiphysis, so most heal with normal growth (Salter-Harris I and II).

### Peripheral structures
- **Groove (ossification groove) of Ranvier:** wedge of **chondroprogenitor cells** at the periphery: **growth in width (latitudinal growth)** of the physis.
- **Perichondrial ring of LaCroix:** dense fibrous band continuous with periosteum; **mechanical support** to the physis against shear.

### Regulation of physeal growth
- **Indian hedgehog (IHH) - PTHrP negative feedback loop:** prehypertrophic chondrocytes secrete IHH, which stimulates **PTHrP** at the ends of bone; PTHrP **keeps chondrocytes proliferating and delays hypertrophy**. **Activating PTH/PTHrP receptor mutation = Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia**.
- **FGFR3:** **negative regulator** of proliferation (activating mutation = achondroplasia; vosoritide, a CNP analogue, counteracts it).
- **Growth hormone/IGF-1:** proliferation (GH excess before closure: gigantism; after: acromegaly).
- **Thyroid hormone:** hypertrophy and maturation (hypothyroidism: delayed maturation, SCFE, epiphyseal dysgenesis).
- **Oestrogen:** drives **physeal closure** in both sexes (aromatase or oestrogen-receptor deficiency: tall stature with open physes).
- **Glucocorticoids:** inhibit growth. **Vitamin D, calcium, phosphate:** mineralisation of the hypertrophic zone.
- **Mechanical: Hueter-Volkmann law:** **compression inhibits and tension stimulates physeal growth** (basis of progression of scoliosis, Blount disease, clubfoot deformity, and of **guided growth / hemiepiphysiodesis**).

## 7. Mechanical adaptation and remodelling
- **Wolff's law:** bone **remodels in response to the loads placed on it** (adds bone where stressed, removes it where unloaded: stress shielding under stiff implants, disuse osteoporosis, astronauts).
- **Frost's mechanostat:** bone responds to **strain thresholds**: below a minimum, disuse remodelling (net loss); in the adapted window, maintenance; above, modelling (net gain); far above, microdamage and fracture.
- **Piezoelectricity / electrical properties:** the **compression side is electronegative** (bone **formation**); the **tension side is electropositive** (bone **resorption**); basis of **electrical stimulation** of non-unions (cathode = bone formation).
- **Modelling vs remodelling:**
  - **Modelling** changes shape and size (**formation and resorption on different surfaces**, not coupled), e.g. growth, correction of malunion in children.
  - **Remodelling** replaces old bone with new (**coupled** resorption then formation at the same site), maintains mass and repairs microdamage.

### The remodelling cycle: basic multicellular unit (BMU)
1. **Activation** (osteocyte signals, microdamage; lining cells retract, precursors recruited).
2. **Resorption** by osteoclasts (about **2-4 weeks**).
3. **Reversal** (mononuclear cells clean the surface, lay the cement line; coupling signals released: TGF-beta, IGF, BMPs).
4. **Formation** by osteoblasts (osteoid then mineralisation; about **3-4 months**).
5. **Quiescence** (lining cells).
- **Cortical remodelling:** the **cutting cone** (osteoclasts at the tip boring a tunnel) followed by osteoblasts filling it in (closing cone) to form a new osteon: seen in **primary (direct) bone healing** under absolute stability.
- **Trabecular remodelling:** on surfaces (hemi-osteons).
- **Annual turnover:** roughly **25% of trabecular** bone and about **2-5% of cortical** bone per year in adults (the total skeleton is replaced in about 10 years).
- **Peak bone mass** is reached in the **third decade** (genetics determine most of it; also exercise, calcium, hormones). Thereafter bone is lost slowly in both sexes, **accelerated for 5-10 years after menopause** (oestrogen deficiency: increased RANKL, decreased OPG, longer osteoclast survival).

## 8. Calcium, phosphate and their hormones
### Normal values
- **Serum calcium:** about **8.5-10.5 mg/dL (2.2-2.6 mmol/L)**; about **half ionised** (biologically active), about 40% protein-bound (albumin), the rest complexed. Correct for albumin (add 0.8 mg/dL per 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4). **Alkalosis lowers ionised calcium** (tetany with hyperventilation).
- **Serum phosphate:** about **2.5-4.5 mg/dL** in adults (higher in children).
- **Daily calcium requirement (approximate):** **adults about 1,000 mg**; **adolescents about 1,300 mg**; **postmenopausal women and older adults about 1,200 mg**; pregnancy and lactation need more (ICMR figures for Indians are lower). **Vitamin D:** about **600-800 IU/day** (800-1,000 IU in the elderly and osteoporotic).

### Hormones
| Hormone | Source | Stimulus | Effect on bone | Gut | Kidney |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PTH** (84 amino acids) | **Chief cells** of parathyroid | **Low ionised calcium** (sensed by the **calcium-sensing receptor**), high phosphate | **Resorption (indirect, via osteoblast RANKL)**; intermittent = anabolic | Indirect (via 1,25-D) | **Increases calcium reabsorption** (distal tubule), **increases phosphate excretion** (inhibits proximal reabsorption), **stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase** |
| **1,25(OH)2D (calcitriol)** | Kidney (**1-alpha-hydroxylase**, proximal tubule) | PTH, low phosphate | Mineralisation (supplies calcium and phosphate); RANKL up at high levels | **Increases calcium and phosphate absorption** | Increases calcium reabsorption |
| **Calcitonin** | **Parafollicular C cells** of thyroid | High calcium | **Directly inhibits osteoclasts** | | Increases calcium excretion |
| **FGF23** | **Osteocytes** | High phosphate, 1,25-D | Mineralisation impaired if excess | Reduces phosphate absorption (via low 1,25-D) | **Phosphaturia** (with Klotho), **inhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase** |

- **Vitamin D pathway:** **7-dehydrocholesterol** in skin + **UVB** gives **cholecalciferol (D3)** (or dietary D2/D3); **liver 25-hydroxylase** forms **25(OH)D (calcidiol)**, the **best measure of vitamin D status** (long half-life); **kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase** forms **1,25(OH)2D**, the active hormone; 24-hydroxylase produces inactive 24,25(OH)2D.
- **FGF23 excess:** **X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX)**, autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23 gene), **tumour-induced osteomalacia**; **burosumab** (anti-FGF23 antibody) treats XLH and TIO. FGF23 also rises early in **CKD**.
- **Other hormones on bone:**
  - **Oestrogen/testosterone:** anti-resorptive (oestrogen is key in men too).
  - **Glucocorticoids:** **decrease osteoblast formation and lifespan**, increase osteocyte apoptosis, reduce gut calcium absorption, increase renal loss; **trabecular loss** (vertebral fractures) in the first months; commonest cause of secondary osteoporosis.
  - **Thyroid hormone:** increases turnover and resorption (cortical loss with excess).
  - **Growth hormone/IGF-1, insulin:** anabolic.
  - **Leptin, serotonin, sympathetic tone:** central regulation (research level).

## 9. Bone turnover markers
| Type | Markers |
|---|---|
| **Formation** | **Bone-specific ALP**, **osteocalcin**, **P1NP (procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide)**, P1CP |
| **Resorption** | **Serum CTX (C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen)**, **urinary NTX**, **urinary pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline** (deoxypyridinoline is more bone-specific), urinary **hydroxyproline** (least specific; diet-dependent), **TRAP-5b** |

- **Reference markers recommended by the IOF and IFCC:** **serum P1NP (formation) and serum CTX (resorption)**.
- CTX should be drawn **fasting in the morning** (circadian and food effects).
- **Uses:** monitoring **adherence and response** to treatment (antiresorptives cause CTX to fall within about 3 months; teriparatide raises P1NP), Paget activity (ALP), and research. **Not for diagnosing osteoporosis** and poor at predicting fracture in an individual.

## 10. Bone morphogenetic proteins and growth factors
- **BMPs** belong to the **TGF-beta superfamily**; they signal through **serine-threonine kinase receptors** (type I and II) and intracellular **SMAD** proteins (SMAD 1, 5, 8); inhibited by **noggin**, chordin, gremlin.
- **Osteoinductive:** they cause mesenchymal stem cells to differentiate into bone-forming cells (Urist, 1965: demineralised bone matrix forms ectopic bone).
- **Clinical products:** **rhBMP-2** (open tibial fractures with IM nailing, the **BESTT trial**; anterior lumbar interbody fusion with cages) and **rhBMP-7 (OP-1)** (non-unions; withdrawn from the market). Complications: **heterotopic ossification**, **soft-tissue swelling** (dangerous in **anterior cervical fusion**: airway compromise; FDA warning), seroma, osteolysis, retrograde ejaculation (ALIF), radiculitis; cancer risk debated.
- **ACVR1 (ALK2, a BMP type I receptor) activating mutation = fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva.**
- **Other factors:**
  - **TGF-beta:** stored abundantly in bone matrix; stimulates mesenchymal cell proliferation and matrix synthesis; coupling factor.
  - **PDGF:** from platelets; chemotactic and mitogenic (early fracture haematoma).
  - **IGF-1/2:** stimulate osteoblast collagen synthesis.
  - **FGF:** angiogenesis and mesenchymal proliferation.
  - **VEGF:** angiogenesis (vascular invasion of hypertrophic cartilage, distraction osteogenesis).
  - **Prostaglandin E2:** stimulates both formation and resorption; **NSAIDs (COX-2 inhibition)** impair fracture healing and **prevent heterotopic ossification** (indomethacin).

## 11. Bone graft properties (applied bone biology)
| Property | Meaning | Best source |
|---|---|---|
| **Osteogenesis** | Contains **living cells that form bone** | **Autograft only** (cancellous best), bone marrow aspirate |
| **Osteoinduction** | **Growth factors** induce stem cells to become bone-forming cells | **BMPs**, demineralised bone matrix (DBM), autograft |
| **Osteoconduction** | **Scaffold** for ingrowth of vessels and cells | Autograft, allograft, calcium phosphate, hydroxyapatite, calcium sulfate, tricalcium phosphate |
| **Osteointegration** | Surface bonding of bone to the graft/implant without fibrous tissue | Autograft, HA-coated and porous implants |

- **Autograft (iliac crest)** has **all properties** and is the **gold standard**; cancellous incorporates fastest (creeping substitution), cortical gives strength but is **weakest at about 6 months to 2 years** during revascularisation and resorption before strength returns.
- **Allograft:** osteoconductive (and weakly inductive); **fresh-frozen** retains more strength than freeze-dried (lyophilised, weakest); immunogenicity mainly from **marrow cells** (class I and II MHC); **HIV transmission risk about 1 in 1.6 million** with modern screening (traditional quoted figure). Gamma irradiation over about 25 kGy weakens bone.
- **Vascularised graft** (fibula, iliac crest): heals like a fracture (primary incorporation), no creeping substitution phase, hypertrophies with loading; for **defects over 6 cm**, irradiated beds, osteonecrosis.
- **Masquelet induced-membrane technique:** cement spacer induces a vascular membrane rich in growth factors (VEGF, TGF-beta, BMP-2), peak bioactivity at about **4-8 weeks**; second stage fills it with cancellous graft.

## 12. Bone material properties (summary for biology questions)
- **Anisotropic** (strength depends on load direction: strongest **along the long axis**), **viscoelastic** (stiffer and stronger at **higher loading rates**: high-energy fractures are comminuted).
- **Strongest in compression**, weaker in tension, **weakest in shear**.
- **Young's modulus:** cortical bone about **15-20 GPa**; cancellous much lower; stiffness order of common materials: **ceramic > cobalt-chrome > stainless steel > titanium > cortical bone > PMMA cement > polyethylene > cancellous bone > tendon/ligament > cartilage** (titanium's modulus is closest to bone among metals: less stress shielding).
- **Ageing:** cortical thinning, increased porosity, **endosteal resorption with periosteal apposition** (bone diameter widens to preserve bending strength), more brittle collagen.

> Exam pearl: **Osteoclast** = haematopoietic (monocyte-macrophage) origin, needs **M-CSF + RANKL**, marked by **TRAP**, attaches by **alpha-v-beta-3 integrin**, resorbs via **proton pump, carbonic anhydrase II, cathepsin K**; has **calcitonin receptors but no PTH receptors**. **Osteoblast** = mesenchymal, **RUNX2 then osterix**, Wnt/LRP5 driven, makes **type I collagen, osteocalcin, ALP, RANKL and OPG**. **Osteocyte** = 90-95% of cells, mechanosensor, makes **sclerostin and FGF23**.

> Exam pearl: Physis: **proliferative zone = achondroplasia**; **hypertrophic zone = rickets, SCFE, Salter-Harris fractures, MPS**; **primary spongiosa = scurvy and osteomyelitis**; **secondary spongiosa = osteopetrosis**. **Hueter-Volkmann:** compression slows growth. **Most abundant non-collagenous protein = osteocalcin (vitamin K-dependent)**. Reference turnover markers = **P1NP and CTX**.

> Exam pearl: Normal flow in mature bone is **centrifugal**; after displaced fracture/reaming it becomes **centripetal**. The **nutrient artery supplies the inner two-thirds** of the cortex; **periosteum the outer third**. **Distraction osteogenesis = intramembranous ossification**; **callus = endochondral**.

cartilage and synovium.md:
## 1. Types of cartilage
| Type | Collagen | Sites | Exam point |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hyaline (articular)** | **Type II** | Joint surfaces, physis, costal, tracheal | Avascular, aneural, alymphatic; very limited repair |
| **Fibrocartilage** | **Type I** (dominant) | Meniscus, annulus fibrosus, labrum, TFCC, pubic symphysis, tendon and ligament insertions | Forms the **repair tissue after marrow stimulation**; mechanically inferior to hyaline |
| **Elastic** | Type II plus elastin | Ear, epiglottis | Rarely examined in orthopaedics |
| **Physeal (growth plate)** | Type II, **type X** in hypertrophic zone | Physis | See bone biology notes |

## 2. Composition of articular cartilage
- **Water: about 65-80% of wet weight**
  - Highest at the **surface**, lowest in the deep zone.
  - Held in the matrix by the negative charge of proteoglycans; moves in and out with loading (nutrition and lubrication).
  - **Increased water content = increased permeability, decreased strength and stiffness** (seen in **OA**).
- **Collagen: about 10-20% of wet weight (over half of dry weight)**
  - **Type II = about 90-95%** of cartilage collagen: gives **tensile strength** and holds proteoglycans in place.
  - **Type IX:** cross-links type II fibrils (II-IX-XI network).
  - **Type XI:** regulates fibril size; with II and IX forms the heterotypic fibril.
  - **Type VI:** **pericellular matrix** around chondrocytes; increases early in OA.
  - **Type X:** **calcified cartilage zone and hypertrophic physeal chondrocytes**; associated with mineralisation (Schmid metaphyseal chondrodysplasia = COL10A1).
  - Collagen turnover is **extremely slow** (half-life of many years to decades); once lost it is effectively not replaced.
- **Proteoglycans: about 10-15% of wet weight**
  - Main proteoglycan = **aggrecan**: a **core protein** carrying **glycosaminoglycan (GAG) side chains**: **chondroitin sulfate** (chondroitin-4 and chondroitin-6 sulfate) and **keratan sulfate**.
  - Many aggrecan molecules attach to a long **hyaluronic acid** chain, stabilised by **link protein**, forming huge **aggregates**.
  - GAG chains carry **fixed negative charges** (sulfate and carboxyl groups) that attract cations and water (**Donnan osmotic pressure**): this swelling, resisted by the collagen network, gives **compressive stiffness**.
  - Proteoglycans also **reduce permeability** (keep water in under load).
  - Turnover is much faster than collagen (weeks to months): proteoglycan loss is the earliest and reversible change.
  - Small proteoglycans: **decorin, biglycan, fibromodulin** (bind collagen, regulate fibril formation, bind TGF-beta).
- **Chondrocytes: about 1-5% of volume (about 2% classically quoted)**
  - Derived from mesenchymal stem cells; produce and maintain all matrix (collagen, proteoglycans, enzymes).
  - Live in **lacunae**; **no cell-to-cell contact**; low metabolic rate.
  - Mostly **anaerobic metabolism** (low oxygen tension).
- **Other matrix proteins**
  - **Lubricin (PRG4, superficial zone protein):** secreted by superficial chondrocytes and synoviocytes; **boundary lubricant**.
  - **COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein):** mutations cause **pseudoachondroplasia and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia**; serum COMP is a marker of cartilage turnover.
  - Anchorin CII (chondrocyte attachment), chondronectin, fibronectin.

### Age-related change in GAGs (frequently tested)
- **Chondroitin-4 sulfate decreases with age.**
- **Chondroitin-6 sulfate stays about the same.**
- **Keratan sulfate increases with age.**
- So the **chondroitin : keratan sulfate ratio falls with ageing** but **rises in OA**.

## 3. Zones (layers) of articular cartilage
| Zone | Collagen orientation | Cells | Composition | Function |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Superficial (tangential), about 10-20%** | **Parallel to the surface** | Flattened, elongated, highest density | **Highest water and collagen, lowest proteoglycan**; secretes lubricin | Resists **shear** and tension; the **lamina splendens** (acellular film of fine fibrils) on top |
| **Middle (transitional), 40-60%** | **Oblique / random** | Round, sparse | More proteoglycan | Transition from shear to compression |
| **Deep (radial), about 30%** | **Perpendicular** to the surface | Round, in **vertical columns** | **Highest proteoglycan, lowest water**, largest collagen fibrils | Resists **compression**; collagen anchors across the tidemark |
| **Tidemark** | Basophilic line | None | Boundary between uncalcified and calcified cartilage | **Advances and duplicates in OA and with age** |
| **Calcified cartilage** | Anchoring fibrils | Hypertrophic, few | Hydroxyapatite, **type X collagen** | Anchors cartilage to **subchondral bone** |

- **Cartilage is thickest** where contact stresses are highest (e.g. **patella: up to about 5-7 mm**, the thickest articular cartilage in the body).
- Regionally, the matrix is organised into **pericellular** (type VI collagen, thin), **territorial** and **interterritorial** (largest, most of the bulk, gives mechanical properties) regions.

## 4. Nutrition, metabolism and regulation
- **Avascular:** nutrition by **diffusion from synovial fluid**, helped by **cyclic loading** (pumping of fluid in and out). Immature cartilage also receives some supply from subchondral vessels.
- **Anaerobic glycolysis** is the main energy pathway.
- **Anabolic factors:** **IGF-1** (main anabolic factor in synovial fluid), **TGF-beta**, **BMP-7 (OP-1)**, **FGF-18** (sprifermin, studied as disease-modifying OA drug), PDGF.
- **Catabolic factors:**
  - **IL-1 beta** (most important catabolic cytokine) and **TNF-alpha** from synovium and chondrocytes.
  - Induce **MMPs**: **MMP-13 (collagenase-3)** is the main enzyme degrading **type II collagen**; MMP-1, MMP-3 (stromelysin).
  - **Aggrecanases: ADAMTS-4 and ADAMTS-5** cleave aggrecan (ADAMTS-5 is dominant in animal models).
  - Natural inhibitors: **TIMPs** (tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases), plasmin activator inhibitor.
  - Nitric oxide, prostaglandin E2 add to catabolism.
- **Effect of loading:** normal cyclic loading maintains matrix; **immobilisation** causes proteoglycan loss, softening and thinning (largely reversible early), and **joint contracture and adhesions** with prolonged immobilisation. **Excessive impact load** (over about 25 MPa in experiments) causes chondrocyte death and fissuring.
- **Continuous passive motion (Salter's experiments)** improved healing of full-thickness defects in animals (more hyaline-like repair).

## 5. Biomechanics of cartilage
### Biphasic and viscoelastic material
- **Biphasic:** a **solid phase** (collagen-proteoglycan matrix) and a **fluid phase** (water and ions). Under load, fluid pressurisation carries most of the load initially (**over 90%**), shielding the solid matrix.
- **Viscoelastic** (time-dependent) behaviour:
  - **Creep:** under constant load, deformation increases with time as fluid is exuded.
  - **Stress relaxation:** under constant deformation, stress falls with time.
- **Permeability is low** and **inversely related to proteoglycan content**; it **falls with compression** (strain-dependent permeability), which traps fluid and protects the matrix.
- **Anisotropic** (properties differ by direction and zone) and **inhomogeneous**.
- **Tensile strength** comes from collagen; **compressive stiffness** from proteoglycans and fluid pressure; **shear** resisted by collagen.

### Lubrication (very commonly asked)
- **Coefficient of friction of a synovial joint: about 0.002-0.04** (lower than any man-made bearing; metal-on-polyethylene is about 0.05-0.15).
- **Boundary lubrication:** a monolayer of **lubricin** (glycoprotein) on each surface prevents direct contact; important at **low speed, high load** and **standing**.
- **Fluid-film lubrication:** a film of fluid separates the surfaces; types:
  - **Hydrodynamic:** non-parallel surfaces sliding create a wedge of fluid (rigid bearings).
  - **Elastohydrodynamic:** cartilage deforms, increasing the contact area and trapping fluid; generally regarded as the **main mode during dynamic joint motion**.
  - **Squeeze-film:** surfaces approach each other perpendicularly, squeezing fluid out (heel strike).
  - **Weeping (self-pressurised):** fluid is squeezed out of the cartilage into the gap under load.
  - **Boosted:** solvent passes into the cartilage leaving concentrated **hyaluronic acid-protein gel** pooled between the surfaces.
- **Hyaluronic acid** gives synovial fluid its **viscosity** but contributes less to cartilage-on-cartilage boundary lubrication than lubricin.

### Wear
- **Interfacial wear:** adhesion (surfaces bond and tear) or abrasion (hard surface cuts soft).
- **Fatigue wear:** accumulation of microscopic damage from cyclic loading even with good lubrication.
- Loss of lubricin (e.g. **camptodactyly-arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis syndrome**, PRG4 mutation) causes early joint failure.

## 6. Ageing versus osteoarthritis (most-tested table)
| Parameter | **Ageing** | **Osteoarthritis** |
|---|---|---|
| **Water content** | **Decreased** | **Increased** (early; collagen network failure lets the matrix swell) |
| Collagen | Content similar; **more cross-links, AGEs** (stiffer, brittle) | Network disrupted and **disorganised**; relative content falls late |
| **Proteoglycan content** | Decreased | **Decreased** (progressive) |
| Proteoglycan size and aggregation | Smaller, less aggregated | Shorter chains, less aggregation |
| Chondroitin-4 sulfate | Decreased | **Increased** |
| Keratan sulfate | **Increased** | **Decreased** |
| **Chondrocyte number** | **Decreased** (cells larger) | Early **increased** (cloning, clusters), late decreased |
| Synthetic activity | Decreased | **Increased** early (attempted repair) |
| **Degradative enzymes (MMP, ADAMTS)** | Little change | **Markedly increased** |
| **Modulus of elasticity (stiffness)** | **Increased** | **Decreased** (soft) |
| **Permeability** | Decreased | **Increased** |

- **Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)** accumulate with age (pentosidine), making cartilage stiffer and more brittle and linking ageing to OA risk.

### Pathological sequence in OA
1. **Proteoglycan loss** and increased water (swelling, softening): chondromalacia.
2. **Fibrillation** of the superficial zone, vertical **fissures** (clefts) reaching deeper layers.
3. **Chondrocyte cloning** (clusters), tidemark **duplication and advancement**, vascular invasion of calcified cartilage.
4. Full-thickness loss with **eburnation** of exposed bone.
5. Bone response: **subchondral sclerosis**, **cysts (geodes)** from synovial fluid intrusion, **osteophytes** (endochondral ossification at the margins, TGF-beta driven), bone marrow lesions on MRI.
6. Secondary **synovitis** with IL-1 and TNF release.
- **Radiographic signs (four):** joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts.
- **Kellgren-Lawrence grade:** 0 none; 1 doubtful narrowing, possible osteophyte; 2 definite osteophytes, possible narrowing; 3 multiple osteophytes, definite narrowing, some sclerosis, possible deformity; 4 large osteophytes, marked narrowing, severe sclerosis, definite deformity.

## 7. Cartilage injury and repair
### Response to injury
- **Matrix injury without cell death (blunt load):** chondrocytes can restore proteoglycan if the insult stops.
- **Partial-thickness (superficial) laceration:** **does not cross the tidemark**; no inflammatory response, no blood or stem cells reach it; chondrocytes near the edge proliferate briefly but **the defect does not heal** (and may not progress).
- **Full-thickness (osteochondral) injury:** **penetrates subchondral bone**; bleeding brings a fibrin clot with **marrow mesenchymal stem cells** that form **fibrocartilage (type I collagen)**, which is less stiff, wears out and degenerates over time.
- **Blunt trauma** (impact) can kill chondrocytes and damage the matrix without visible surface damage; associated bone bruises on MRI.

### Grading of chondral lesions
| Grade | **Outerbridge** (arthroscopic) | **ICRS** |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Normal | Normal |
| **1** | **Softening and swelling** | Nearly normal: soft indentation and/or superficial fissures and cracks |
| **2** | Fragmentation and fissuring **under 1.3 cm (half an inch)** diameter | Abnormal: lesion extends **under 50% of cartilage depth** |
| **3** | Fragmentation and fissuring **over 1.3 cm** diameter | Severely abnormal: **over 50% depth** (3a), down to calcified layer (3b), down to but not through subchondral bone (3c), blisters (3d) |
| **4** | **Erosion down to exposed subchondral bone** | Severely abnormal: **through the subchondral bone** (osteochondral) |

- **MRI:** fat-suppressed proton density / fast spin echo sequences best for cartilage; T2 mapping and dGEMRIC (proteoglycan content) are research and early-OA tools.

### Surgical repair options
| Technique | Principle | Tissue formed | Best indication | Key points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Debridement / chondroplasty** | Remove unstable flaps | None | Symptomatic loose flaps | Palliative |
| **Marrow stimulation: microfracture** (Steadman), drilling, abrasion | Breach subchondral plate; marrow clot with MSCs | **Fibrocartilage (type I)** | **Small contained defects, under about 2-4 cm2**, low-demand, femoral condyle | Awl holes **about 3-4 mm apart**, perpendicular, **remove calcified cartilage layer**, keep subchondral plate bridges; protected weight bearing about 6 weeks and CPM; results deteriorate after about 5 years; may impair later ACI (intralesional osteophytes) |
| **Osteochondral autograft (OATS, mosaicplasty)** | Transfer cylindrical plugs from non-weight-bearing area (intercondylar notch, trochlear margins) | **Hyaline cartilage** with bone | **Small defects (about 1-4 cm2)**, young patients, single stage | **Donor-site morbidity** limits size; plugs flush with surface (proud plugs fail); fibrocartilage fills gaps between plugs |
| **Osteochondral allograft (fresh)** | Size-matched graft from cadaver | Hyaline with **viable chondrocytes** | **Large defects (over about 2-4 cm2), bone loss** (OCD, AVN, salvage) | Chondrocyte viability falls with storage (use within about 28 days of harvest); disease transmission risk small; immunogenicity low (cartilage relatively immunoprivileged) |
| **Autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI / MACI)** | **Two-stage:** arthroscopic biopsy, cells expanded in culture, implanted under a cover | **Hyaline-like** cartilage | **Larger defects (about 2-10 cm2)**, young active patients, failed microfracture | 1st generation **periosteal patch: hypertrophy** (commonest complication); 2nd generation collagen membrane; 3rd **matrix-induced (MACI)**: cells seeded on a scaffold, arthroscopic or mini-open implantation |
| Scaffold-based one-stage (AMIC, particulated juvenile cartilage, BST-CarGel) | Augmented marrow stimulation | Fibrocartilage / hyaline-like | Medium defects | Evidence developing |

- **SUMMIT trial (Saris et al., 2014):** for symptomatic knee cartilage defects **of 3 cm2 or more**, **MACI was superior to microfracture** at 2 years (pain and function).
- Treat **malalignment (HTO/DFO), instability (ACL) and meniscal deficiency** at the same time; otherwise any cartilage procedure fails.
- **Contraindications:** inflammatory arthritis, bipolar (kissing) lesions (relative), established OA, uncorrected malalignment, obesity (relative).

## 8. The synovium
### Structure
- **Synovial membrane** lines the joint capsule, tendon sheaths and bursae (not the articular cartilage or meniscal surfaces).
- **Intima:** 1-4 cell layers of synoviocytes; **no basement membrane, no tight junctions**: allows free exchange between blood and synovial fluid.
- **Subintima:** loose connective tissue (areolar, fibrous or fatty), **highly vascular** (fenestrated capillaries), lymphatics and nerves.
- **Synoviocytes:**
  - **Type A (macrophage-like):** derived from **bone marrow (monocyte lineage)**; **phagocytic**, clear debris; antigen-presenting; express CD68.
  - **Type B (fibroblast-like):** mesenchymal; **produce hyaluronic acid and lubricin**, collagen, fibronectin; key effector cells of **rheumatoid pannus** (invade cartilage).
  - Type C: intermediate forms.
- **Functions:** produce synovial fluid components, nourish cartilage, remove debris, regulate fluid volume, immune surveillance.

### Synovial fluid
- **Ultrafiltrate (dialysate) of plasma plus hyaluronic acid and lubricin** secreted by type B cells.
- **Does not normally clot:** contains **no fibrinogen** or clotting factors (large proteins excluded); inflammation lets fibrinogen in, so inflammatory fluid can clot.
- Small molecules (glucose, electrolytes) equilibrate with plasma; **glucose about equal to plasma** normally; **low glucose in septic and sometimes rheumatoid** fluid.
- **Non-Newtonian, thixotropic (shear-thinning):** **viscosity falls as shear rate rises**; due to hyaluronic acid. Viscosity also falls when hyaluronic acid is degraded or diluted (inflammation): **poor string sign**.
- **Normal knee volume: under about 4 mL**; clear, pale yellow; **WBC under 200/mm3**, under 25% neutrophils.
- **Total protein** about one-third of plasma; immunoglobulins and albumin present.

### Synovial fluid analysis
| Category | Appearance | Viscosity | **WBC / mm3** | **% neutrophils** | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Normal** | Clear, straw | High | **Under 200** | Under 25% | |
| **Non-inflammatory** | Clear, yellow | High | **200-2,000** | Under 25% | OA, trauma, AVN, neuropathic joint |
| **Inflammatory** | Cloudy, yellow | Low | **2,000-50,000** (up to about 75,000) | Over 50% | RA, gout, pseudogout, spondyloarthropathy, reactive |
| **Septic** | Turbid, purulent | Variable | **Over 50,000** (often over 100,000) | **Over 75-90%** | Bacterial arthritis (glucose low, lactate high) |
| **Haemorrhagic** | Bloody | Variable | Variable | | Trauma (ACL tear, fracture: **fat globules = intra-articular fracture**), haemophilia, PVNS, anticoagulation, tumour |

- **Crystals (compensated polarised light microscopy):**

| Crystal | Disease | Shape | Birefringence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Monosodium urate** | Gout | **Needle-shaped** | **Strongly negative** (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis) |
| **Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD)** | Pseudogout, chondrocalcinosis | **Rhomboid / rod-shaped** | **Weakly positive** (blue when parallel) |
| Basic calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) | Calcific tendinitis, Milwaukee shoulder | Clumps, not seen individually | Not birefringent; **Alizarin red** stain |
| Cholesterol | Chronic effusions (RA) | Flat notched plates | Variable |
| Calcium oxalate | Renal failure | Bipyramidal | Positive |

- **Crystals do not exclude infection**: gout and septic arthritis can coexist; always culture.
- **Prosthetic joint (ICM 2018 minor criteria):** chronic PJI synovial **WBC over 3,000/mm3** and **PMN over 80%**; acute (under about 6 weeks post-op) **WBC over 10,000** and **PMN over 90%**; also **alpha-defensin** and **leukocyte esterase (++)**.

## 9. Synovial and inflammatory conditions (exam-relevant)
### Inflammatory synovitis
- **Rheumatoid arthritis:** synovial hyperplasia, lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration, angiogenesis; **pannus** (type B synoviocytes, macrophages) erodes cartilage and bone at the **bare areas** (marginal erosions); osteoclasts activated by **RANKL**.
  - Cartilage destruction by **MMPs, IL-1, TNF-alpha**: basis of biological therapy (anti-TNF, IL-6 blockade, JAK inhibitors).
  - Radiographs: periarticular osteopenia, symmetric joint space narrowing, marginal erosions (contrast OA: asymmetric narrowing, osteophytes, sclerosis).
- **Haemophilic synovitis:** recurrent haemarthrosis, **iron (haemosiderin) deposition** in synovium causes hypertrophic synovitis and **direct chondrocyte toxicity**; target joint knee, elbow, ankle; treatment factor replacement, **radiosynovectomy** or arthroscopic synovectomy, later arthroplasty. Arnold-Hilgartner and Pettersson classifications.

### Proliferative synovial lesions
| Condition | Key features | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)** | Benign neoplasm with **CSF1 gene translocation** (overexpression of CSF1 recruits macrophages); **knee commonest** (then hip); **localised** (nodular, mechanical symptoms) or **diffuse** (recurrent **haemorrhagic effusion**, brown fluid); erosions on both sides of the joint (hip); **MRI: low signal on T1 and T2, "blooming" on gradient-echo** from haemosiderin | Localised: arthroscopic or open excision (low recurrence). Diffuse: **complete synovectomy** (open or combined anterior-posterior), recurrence high (up to about 30-50%); adjuvant radiotherapy; **pexidartinib (CSF1R inhibitor)** for unresectable disease |
| **Synovial chondromatosis** | Synovial metaplasia forming **cartilaginous loose bodies** (many, similar size); **knee, hip, elbow**; primary is a neoplasm (FN1-ACVR2A fusion); **Milgram stages**: 1 active synovial disease without loose bodies, 2 transitional (both), 3 loose bodies only, quiescent synovium | Removal of loose bodies **plus synovectomy** (stages 1-2); recurrence possible; rare **chondrosarcoma** transformation |
| **Lipoma arborescens** | Villous fatty proliferation of synovium; suprapatellar pouch; MRI fat signal fronds | Synovectomy |
| **Synovial haemangioma** | Child or young adult knee; recurrent haemarthrosis | Excision |

- **Synovial sarcoma is not a synovial tumour** (arises near, not in, joints; t(X;18) SS18-SSX).

### Differential distractors
- **Loose bodies:** OCD fragment, osteochondral fracture, synovial chondromatosis, OA osteophytes, rice bodies (RA, TB), lipoma arborescens.
- **Recurrent haemarthrosis:** haemophilia, PVNS, synovial haemangioma, anticoagulation, neuropathic joint, sickle cell.

## 10. Treatment-related science (frequently asked)
- **Intra-articular corticosteroids:** short-term pain relief; repeated injections may accelerate cartilage loss (McAlindon 2017: triamcinolone every 3 months for 2 years gave greater cartilage volume loss and no pain benefit over saline). Avoid within about 3 months before arthroplasty (infection risk).
- **Intra-articular hyaluronic acid (viscosupplementation):** restores viscosity briefly; **AAOS knee OA guideline (2021): not recommended for routine use**.
- **Glucosamine and chondroitin:** substrates for GAG synthesis; high-quality trials (e.g. GAIT) show little or no benefit over placebo overall; not recommended by AAOS.
- **Platelet-rich plasma:** growth factors (PDGF, TGF-beta, VEGF); some evidence of benefit in knee OA; guideline recommendations limited/variable (debated).
- **NSAIDs:** inhibit COX and prostaglandins; first-line drug therapy along with exercise and weight loss (strong evidence).
- **Local anaesthetics** (bupivacaine, especially continuous intra-articular infusion via pain pumps) are **chondrotoxic**: **post-arthroscopic glenohumeral chondrolysis**.
- **Fluoroquinolones** damage developing cartilage in animals (and tendons in adults).
- **Gentamicin, chlorhexidine (concentrated)** and some irrigants are also chondrotoxic.
- **Temperature:** radiofrequency ablation can cause chondrocyte death in deep layers.

> Exam pearl: **Cartilage = water 65-80%, type II collagen (tensile strength), aggrecan proteoglycan (compressive stiffness), chondrocytes 1-5%.** Superficial zone: collagen parallel, most water, least proteoglycan, lubricin. Deep zone: perpendicular collagen, most proteoglycan. **Type X collagen = calcified zone and hypertrophic physis.**

> Exam pearl: **Ageing: water down, stiffness up, keratan sulfate up. OA: water UP, stiffness down, permeability up, enzymes (MMP-13, ADAMTS-4/5, IL-1) up, chondrocytes clone early.** Superficial defects do not heal; defects breaching subchondral bone heal with **type I fibrocartilage**.

> Exam pearl: **Synovial fluid has no fibrinogen (does not clot), is thixotropic (viscosity falls with shear, due to hyaluronic acid). Type A synoviocyte = macrophage (marrow-derived); type B = fibroblast (hyaluronic acid, lubricin).** Gout = needle, strongly negative; CPPD = rhomboid, weakly positive. Septic = over 50,000 WBC with over 75-90% neutrophils.

biomechanics and biomaterials.md:
## 1. Basic mechanics
- **Scalar** (magnitude only: mass, speed, energy) vs **vector** (magnitude and direction: force, velocity, moment).
- **Newton's laws:** (1) a body stays at rest or uniform motion unless acted on by a force; (2) **F = ma**; (3) every action has an equal and opposite reaction (basis of **joint reaction force**).
- **Moment (torque) = force x perpendicular distance** from the axis (lever arm); unit **N.m**.
- **Static equilibrium:** sum of forces = 0 and sum of moments = 0; solved with a **free-body diagram**.
- **Levers:**

| Class | Arrangement | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **First** | Fulcrum between effort and load | Head on the atlas (neck extensors), **hip abductors in single-leg stance** |
| **Second** | Load between fulcrum and effort | Standing on tiptoe (fulcrum at MTP joints) |
| **Third** (commonest in body) | Effort between fulcrum and load | **Biceps flexing the elbow**: favours speed and range over force |

- **Work = force x distance (joules)**; **power** = work / time; **kinetic energy = half m v squared**: energy (and so fracture comminution and soft-tissue damage) rises with the **square of velocity** (high-energy and gunshot injuries).

## 2. Material properties
### Stress and strain
- **Stress = force / area** (N/m2 = pascal; MPa, GPa). Normal (tension, compression) or shear.
- **Strain = change in length / original length** (dimensionless or %).
- **Stress-strain curve (tension):**
  1. **Elastic region:** linear, deformation fully recoverable; slope = **Young's modulus of elasticity (E) = stiffness of the material**.
  2. **Proportional limit / yield point:** end of elastic behaviour.
  3. **Plastic region:** permanent deformation (plate contouring happens here).
  4. **Ultimate tensile strength:** maximum stress on the curve.
  5. **Breaking (failure) point.**
- **Strength:** stress at yield or failure. **Stiffness:** resistance to deformation (modulus). They are different: glass is stiff but weak in tension; a material can be strong but flexible.
- **Toughness = area under the stress-strain curve** = energy absorbed before failure.
- **Ductile** materials undergo large plastic deformation before failure (metals, especially stainless steel); **brittle** materials fail with little or no plastic deformation (ceramics, PMMA, glass, cortical bone relatively).
- **Hardness:** resistance to surface indentation and scratching (ceramics hardest): important for bearing surfaces.
- **Poisson's ratio:** lateral strain / axial strain.
- **Fatigue failure:** failure under **repetitive loading below the ultimate strength**; the **endurance limit** is the stress below which a material can withstand an infinite number of cycles (S-N curve). **Most implant failures (plates, nails, stems) are fatigue failures**: an implant that does not heal will eventually break (race between healing and fatigue).
- **Notch sensitivity:** scratches, holes and sharp corners concentrate stress (**stress risers**); **titanium is notch sensitive** (do not bend back and forth or scratch).

### Relative modulus of elasticity (frequently tested order)
| Material | Approximate E |
|---|---|
| **Ceramic (alumina)** | About 350-400 GPa (highest) |
| **Cobalt-chrome alloy** | About 210-230 GPa |
| **Stainless steel (316L)** | About 190-200 GPa |
| **Titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V)** | About 110 GPa |
| **Cortical bone** | About 15-20 GPa |
| **PMMA bone cement** | About 2-3 GPa |
| **UHMWPE** | About 1 GPa |
| **Cancellous bone** | About 0.1-1 GPa (highly variable) |
| Tendon and ligament | Lower still |
| **Articular cartilage** | Lowest (MPa range) |

- **Order to remember: ceramic > CoCr > stainless steel > titanium > cortical bone > PMMA > polyethylene > cancellous bone > tendon/ligament > cartilage.**
- **Titanium is closest to bone**: less stress shielding.

### Viscoelasticity, anisotropy
- **Viscoelastic** materials (bone, ligament, tendon, cartilage) have **time- and rate-dependent** behaviour:
  - **Creep** (deformation increases under constant load), **stress relaxation** (stress falls under constant strain), **hysteresis** (energy lost in loading-unloading cycle).
  - **Faster loading = stiffer and stronger** bone and ligament, more energy absorbed, so high-energy fractures are more comminuted. Ligaments fail mid-substance at fast loading and by avulsion at slow loading.
- **Isotropic:** same properties in all directions (most metals). **Anisotropic:** depends on loading direction (**bone, ligament, cartilage**).
- **Bone is strongest in compression, weaker in tension, weakest in shear**; strongest when loaded along its long axis.

## 3. Bone biomechanics and fracture patterns
| Load | Fracture pattern |
|---|---|
| **Tension** | **Transverse** (avulsion fractures, e.g. patella, olecranon, base of 5th metatarsal) |
| **Compression** | **Oblique** (about 45 degrees, shear plane) or crush/impaction (vertebral body, tibial plateau) |
| **Torsion** | **Spiral** (bone fails in tension along a 45-degree helix) |
| **Bending** | **Transverse**, often with a **butterfly fragment on the compression side** (concave side) |
| Bending + axial compression | Oblique transverse or butterfly |

- **Cortical vs cancellous:** cortical bone is stiffer and stronger but fails at **about 2% strain**; **cancellous bone tolerates up to about 75% strain** before failure (more porous, energy absorbing).
- **Bone density:** compressive strength is roughly proportional to the **square of apparent density**; stiffness to its square or cube.
- **Area moment of inertia (bending) and polar moment of inertia (torsion):** depend on how material is distributed around the neutral axis. For a cylinder, **stiffness and strength are proportional to radius to the fourth power** (r4). With ageing, the cortex thins but **periosteal expansion increases diameter**, partly preserving bending strength.
- **Stress risers in bone:**
  - A screw hole or defect **concentrates stress**; after implant removal, protect the limb until holes fill (about 4-6 months as quoted).
  - An **open-section defect** (a longitudinal slot, e.g. after a cortical window or biopsy) **reduces torsional strength drastically** (by well over half; up to about 90% quoted), far more than a round hole. **Biopsy holes should be round or oval** with rounded ends.
  - Defects **over about 20-30% of bone diameter** substantially weaken the bone; **Mirels' score** guides prophylactic fixation of metastatic lesions (score of 9 or more: fix; 8 borderline; 7 or less: radiotherapy and observe).

## 4. Fracture fixation biomechanics
### Strain theory (Perren)
- **Interfragmentary strain = change in gap width / original gap width.**
  - **Under 2%:** primary (direct) bone healing by cutting cones: needs **absolute stability** (compression plating, lag screws).
  - **2-10%:** secondary (indirect) healing with **callus**: **relative stability** (nails, bridge plates, external fixators, casts).
  - **Over 10%:** granulation tissue only: **non-union** (hypertrophic if biology is good).
- A **single small gap** with motion has **high strain** (bad); spreading movement over a **comminuted zone** lowers strain (why bridge plating works for comminution, and why a simple fracture with a small gap under a bridge plate may not heal).

### Screws
- **Pitch:** distance between adjacent threads; **lead:** distance advanced per turn.
- **Pull-out strength** depends on **outer (thread) diameter**, thread depth, **bone density** (most important clinically) and length of thread engagement. Cancellous screws have larger outer diameter and deeper threads.
- **Bending and torsional strength** of the screw depend on the **core (root) diameter** (proportional to its **cube**).
- **Lag screw** (by design or by technique: glide hole the size of the outer diameter in the near cortex, pilot hole in the far cortex) produces **interfragmentary compression**; placed perpendicular to the fracture for maximum compression, perpendicular to the long axis for resistance to axial load (bisect in practice).
- **Locking screws:** threaded head locks into the plate: **fixed-angle device**; stability does not rely on plate-bone friction; better in **osteoporotic bone, metaphyseal comminution, short segments**, and preserve periosteal blood supply. Fail by **cut-out of the whole construct** rather than sequential screw toggling.

### Plates
- **Bending stiffness of a plate is proportional to its thickness cubed.**
- Functions: **compression** (dynamic compression: eccentric screw in an inclined hole), **neutralisation** (protects lag screws), **buttress** (antiglide; resists shear in metaphyseal fractures), **tension band** (placed on the **tension side**: converts tensile forces into compression; e.g. lateral femur, olecranon wiring), **bridging** (spans comminution).
- **Working length** (distance between the screws closest to the fracture): **longer working length = more flexible** construct and spread strain; leaving 1-2 holes empty either side of a simple fracture in bridge plating is commonly advised; long plates with fewer, well-spaced screws (**plate span width ratio over about 2-3; screw density under about 0.4-0.5**, AO).
- **Plate on the compression side or with a gap opposite (no cortical contact)** sees large bending loads: fatigue failure.
- **Far cortical locking** and dynamic locking screws reduce near-cortex stiffness to promote callus (concept).

### Intramedullary nails
- **Load-sharing** device (vs plates: load bearing or sharing depending on cortical contact).
- **Bending stiffness proportional to radius to the 4th power** (solid) and torsional stiffness depends on polar moment of inertia: a small increase in diameter gives a large increase in stiffness.
- **Slotted (open-section) nails** have much lower torsional stiffness than closed-section nails.
- **Working length** (unsupported length between proximal and distal points of fixation in bone): **torsional stiffness inversely proportional to working length**; **bending stiffness inversely proportional to its square**.
- **Reaming:** allows larger, stronger nail and more cortical contact; reaming products are osteoinductive; **SPRINT trial**: no overall difference between reamed and unreamed tibial nailing for open fractures, possible benefit of reaming in closed fractures (fewer reoperations).
- **Interlocking screws** control rotation and length; **dynamisation** (removing static screws) increases axial loading. Distal locking screw failure is a common fatigue failure in delayed union.

### External fixators: ways to increase stiffness
1. **Increase pin diameter** (most important: **stiffness proportional to pin radius to the fourth power**).
2. **Add more pins** (and use bicortical pins).
3. **Pins close to the fracture** and **far apart from each other within each fragment** ("near-near, far-far").
4. **Bar closer to the bone.**
5. **Add a second bar** (stacked) or a **second plane** (biplanar/multiplanar frames).
6. **Larger-diameter, stiffer connecting rods** (carbon fibre rods are stiff and radiolucent).
7. Ring fixators: more wires, **wire crossing angle near 90 degrees**, **wire tensioning (about 90-130 kg)**, larger wire diameter, smaller ring diameter, more rings, olive wires.
- **Hydroxyapatite-coated pins** reduce loosening.

### Tension band and wire
- **Tension band principle (Pauwels):** an eccentrically loaded bone has a tension and a compression side; an implant on the tension side converts tension into compression at the fracture (olecranon, patella, greater trochanter, medial malleolus). Patellar tension band works best with knee flexion.
- **Wire strength proportional to radius squared** (cross-sectional area); twisting weakens wire; cerclage cables stronger and less prone to loosening than monofilament.

## 5. Joint biomechanics
### Hip
- **Single-leg stance:** body weight (about **five-sixths of BW** acting at the centre of gravity, medial to the hip) is balanced by **abductor force** acting through a much shorter lever arm (body weight lever arm about **2-2.5 times** the abductor lever arm).
- **Joint reaction force (JRF) about 2.5-3 x body weight in single-leg stance**; up to about **5-6 x BW running**, higher in stumbling.
- **Ways to reduce hip JRF:**
  - **Cane in the contralateral hand** (long lever arm from the hip): **reduces JRF by up to about 40-60%** (commonly quoted).
  - **Carry loads in the ipsilateral hand**; a load in the contralateral hand increases JRF greatly.
  - **Weight loss** (each kilogram lost removes about 3 kg from the hip in stance).
  - **Medialise the acetabular component** (shorter body-weight lever arm).
  - **Increase femoral offset or lateralise the greater trochanter** (longer abductor lever arm).
  - **Trendelenburg lurch** (leaning over the affected hip) moves the centre of gravity over the hip and reduces abductor demand.
- **Femoral anteversion and offset** also affect stability and wear; excessive offset increases torsional loads on the stem.

### Knee and patellofemoral joint
- **Tibiofemoral JRF: about 2-4 x BW in walking**; medial compartment carries **about 60-70%** of load in a neutral knee (varus increases this).
- **Patellofemoral JRF:** about **0.5 x BW level walking**, about **3-3.5 x BW stairs**, up to about **7-8 x BW deep squatting**; rises with **knee flexion** and quadriceps force.
- **Patella increases the quadriceps lever arm** (moment arm), most important in the last degrees of extension; **patellectomy reduces extension strength substantially** (often quoted about 25-50%).
- **Screw-home mechanism:** external rotation of the tibia in the last 15-20 degrees of extension; **popliteus unlocks** the knee.
- Q angle: normal about **14 degrees (males) and 17 degrees (females)**; increased Q angle increases lateral patellar force.

### Shoulder, elbow, spine, ankle
- **Glenohumeral JRF about 0.9 x BW at 90 degrees of abduction** (deltoid force); concavity compression by the rotator cuff is the main dynamic stabiliser.
- **Elbow:** load bearing about **60% radiocapitellar, 40% ulnohumeral** (commonly quoted); radial head is a secondary valgus stabiliser (MCL anterior bundle primary).
- **Ankle JRF about 3-5 x BW** in walking; small contact area means high contact stress; **1 mm lateral talar shift reduces tibiotalar contact area by about 42%** (Ramsey and Hamilton).
- **Spine (Nachemson):** L3 intradiscal pressure **lowest lying supine**, higher standing, **higher sitting than standing**, **highest sitting and leaning forward with a weight**.
- **Instantaneous centre of rotation:** many joints (knee) rotate about a shifting centre; surfaces glide and roll.

## 6. Biomaterials: metals
| Metal | Composition | Strengths | Weaknesses / exam points |
|---|---|---|---|
| **316L stainless steel** | Iron with **chromium (about 17-19%)**, **nickel (about 13-15%)**, molybdenum; **L = low carbon** (reduces corrosion) | Cheap, **ductile** (contours well), strong, stiff | **Most corrosion-prone** of implant metals (crevice, pitting); **nickel sensitivity**; stiff (stress shielding); poor fatigue compared with Ti in some settings |
| **Cobalt-chromium (CoCrMo)** | Cobalt, **chromium (about 27-30%)**, molybdenum | **Very hard, wear resistant, strong, excellent corrosion resistance**: **bearing surfaces** (femoral heads, TKA femoral components) | Very stiff (stress shielding); **metal ion release** (Co, Cr) from MoM bearings and taper junctions; cobalt toxicity (cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, hypothyroidism) |
| **Titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V)** | Titanium, aluminium 6%, vanadium 4% | **Lowest modulus (closest to bone)**, **most biocompatible**, best corrosion resistance (passive TiO2 layer), excellent fatigue strength, **osseointegration** | **Poor wear resistance (soft): not used as a bearing surface**; **notch sensitive**; cold-welding of locking screws; galling |
| Commercially pure titanium | Ti | Porous coatings, fibre metal | Weaker than alloy |
| **Tantalum (trabecular metal)** | Porous tantalum on vitreous carbon scaffold | **Porosity about 75-80%**, modulus similar to cancellous bone, **high coefficient of friction** (initial stability), excellent bone ingrowth | Revision acetabular augments and cones; expensive |
| **Nitinol** | Nickel-titanium | **Shape memory and superelasticity** | Staples, wires |
| **Oxidised zirconium (Oxinium)** | Zirconium alloy with surface ceramic conversion | Ceramic-like hard surface on metal core; low PE wear; less brittle | Surface can be breached by dislocation/abrasion |

### Corrosion
- **Passivation:** a protective oxide layer (chromium oxide on steel and CoCr; titanium oxide on Ti) prevents corrosion.

| Type | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Galvanic** | **Two dissimilar metals** in an electrolyte | **Stainless steel with CoCr** (avoid); Ti with CoCr is generally regarded as acceptable |
| **Crevice** | Low-oxygen fissures (no passive layer regeneration) | **Screw-plate interface**; commonest in **316L stainless steel** |
| **Fretting** | Micromotion damages the passive layer repeatedly | Screw heads, **modular tapers** |
| **Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion (MACC, trunnionosis)** | Fretting plus crevice at **head-neck taper** (especially CoCr head on Ti stem, large heads) | **Raised serum cobalt more than chromium**, ALTR/pseudotumour with MoP bearings |
| Pitting | Local breakdown of passive layer | Stainless steel |
| Intergranular, stress, inclusion | Impurities, manufacturing defects, cyclic stress | |

## 7. Biomaterials: polymers
### UHMWPE (ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene)
- Long-chain polymer of ethylene; tough, ductile, **low friction against metal or ceramic**, but **wears**.
- **Sterilisation and oxidation:**
  - **Gamma irradiation in air** creates **free radicals** that **oxidise** the polyethylene over time (shelf ageing): lower toughness, **fatigue cracking, delamination, pitting** (classic failure of 1990s TKA inserts).
  - Current: irradiate in **inert gas or vacuum**, or **ethylene oxide / gas plasma** (no cross-linking).
- **Highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE):** **higher-dose irradiation (about 5-10 Mrad)** creates cross-links that **greatly reduce adhesive/abrasive wear** in THA, then thermal treatment to reduce free radicals:
  - **Remelting** (above the melting point): eliminates free radicals but **reduces fatigue strength, toughness and yield strength**.
  - **Annealing** (below the melting point): preserves mechanical properties but leaves residual free radicals (oxidation risk).
  - **Vitamin E (antioxidant) doping or blending:** stabilises free radicals without remelting.
  - HXLPE greatly reduces osteolysis in THA; in TKA (fatigue-dominated wear) its advantage is less clear.
- **Wear mechanisms:** **adhesion** (main mechanism in THA; material transferred), **abrasion** (third-body or rough counterface), **fatigue** (delamination, pitting: dominant in **TKA** with high contact stress, thin, conforming issues).
- **Wear modes (McKellop):** **mode 1** = intended bearing surfaces; **mode 2** = primary surface against a non-intended surface (head penetrating through liner onto shell); **mode 3** = intended surfaces with **third-body** particles; **mode 4** = two non-intended surfaces rubbing (backside wear, neck-rim impingement, taper).
- **Osteolysis:** **submicron particles (about 0.1-1 micrometre)** are phagocytosed by **macrophages**: release **TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, PGE2, RANKL** activating osteoclasts. Conventional PE linear wear **over about 0.1 mm/year** is associated with osteolysis (threshold often quoted at 0.1-0.2 mm/year).
- **Design rules:**
  - **TKA tibial polyethylene at least about 6-8 mm thick** (8 mm commonly quoted) to limit contact stress and fatigue; more conforming surfaces reduce contact stress.
  - **Larger femoral heads increase volumetric wear** with conventional PE (volumetric wear proportional to radius squared x linear wear) but improve stability; HXLPE allows larger heads.

### PMMA (polymethylmethacrylate) bone cement
- **Two components:**
  - **Powder:** pre-polymerised PMMA, **benzoyl peroxide (initiator)**, **radiopacifier (barium sulfate or zirconium dioxide)**, ± antibiotic.
  - **Liquid:** **MMA monomer**, **N,N-dimethyl-p-toluidine (DMPT, accelerator)**, **hydroquinone (stabiliser/inhibitor, prevents premature polymerisation)**.
- **Exothermic** polymerisation (can reach about 70-80 C or more in thick mantles; thermal necrosis of bone).
- Phases: mixing (wetting), waiting (dough), working, setting. **Higher temperature and humidity shorten setting time**; cooling the monomer lengthens working time.
- **Acts as a grout, not a glue**: mechanical interlock with cancellous bone.
- **Strongest in compression, weak in tension, weakest in shear**; low modulus (2-3 GPa) between metal and bone; **viscoelastic** (creep: allows taper-slip stems to subside).
- **Reducing porosity (vacuum mixing or centrifugation) increases fatigue strength**; antibiotic in high doses reduces strength; **adding liquid antibiotic weakens cement**.
- **Cement mantle at least about 2 mm** and uniform; thin or deficient mantles crack.
- **Cementing generations:**

| Generation | Technique |
|---|---|
| **1st** | Hand mixing, **finger packing**, no canal preparation |
| **2nd** | **Cement gun (retrograde filling), distal canal plug, canal brushing and lavage** |
| **3rd** | 2nd plus **vacuum mixing / centrifugation (reduced porosity), pressurisation, pulsatile lavage**, proximal seal |
| **4th** | 3rd plus **proximal and distal centralisers** (uniform mantle) |

- **Bone cement implantation syndrome:** hypoxia, hypotension, arrhythmia, cardiac arrest at cementation (fat and marrow emboli from pressurisation; monomer contributes); highest risk in **cemented hemiarthroplasty for hip fracture** in frail patients. Measures: lavage, venting, good communication, careful pressurisation.
- **Antibiotic cement:** must be **heat stable, water soluble, powder form, broad spectrum** (gentamicin, tobramycin, vancomycin). Elution is mostly from the surface and early; high-porosity cement elutes more (spacers).

### Other polymers
- **Biodegradable implants: PLLA, PGA, PLGA, polydioxanone** (pins, anchors, interference screws): **PGA** degrades fastest and caused **sterile sinus and foreign-body reactions**; tunnel widening and cyst formation with some anchors.
- **PEEK:** modulus close to bone, radiolucent; spinal cages and anchors.
- **Silicone:** finger joint spacers (Swanson); **silicone synovitis** from particles.

## 8. Biomaterials: ceramics and bearings
- **Ceramics:** **alumina (aluminium oxide)**, **zirconia**, **zirconia-toughened alumina (BIOLOX delta, 4th generation; pink)**.
  - **Hardest, most scratch-resistant, lowest wear**; **hydrophilic (wettable)** surfaces: better lubrication; **biologically inert** particles.
  - **Brittle (low fracture toughness), high modulus**: risk of **fracture** (head or liner; modern fracture rates very low), **chipping** at insertion (liner malseating), **squeaking** (CoC: edge loading, malposition), cannot be contoured.
  - After ceramic fracture, **revise with a ceramic head** (residual ceramic particles destroy a metal head: catastrophic wear) and complete synovectomy.
  - **Zirconia** (pure) had phase transformation and fracture problems (Prozyr recall, 2001).
- **Calcium phosphates (hydroxyapatite, beta-tricalcium phosphate)**, **calcium sulfate**: **osteoconductive** bone graft substitutes; HA coating on uncemented stems; calcium sulfate resorbs fastest (weeks), HA slowest (years); weak in shear and tension: need protected loading.

### Bearing comparison
| Bearing | Wear | Problems |
|---|---|---|
| **Metal-on-conventional PE** | Highest (about 0.1-0.2 mm/year) | Osteolysis |
| **Metal-on-HXLPE** | Very low | Rim fracture with thin liners, malposition |
| **Ceramic-on-PE** | Lower than metal-on-PE | Ceramic fracture (rare) |
| **Metal-on-metal** | Low volumetric wear but **nanometre-sized particles, metal ions** | **ALVAL (lymphocyte-dominated, type IV hypersensitivity)**, **pseudotumour / adverse reaction to metal debris**, raised blood **Co and Cr** (**MHRA concern threshold about 7 ppb, i.e. 7 micrograms/L**); **ASR recall (2010)**; worse in **women, small heads, cup inclination over about 55 degrees** (edge loading); contraindicated in renal failure and women of childbearing age (ions cross placenta) |
| **Ceramic-on-ceramic** | **Lowest wear** | Squeaking, fracture, chipping |

- **Lubrication of bearings:** **lambda ratio** = fluid film thickness / combined surface roughness: **lambda over 3 = full fluid-film lubrication** (CoC, MoM large heads); under 1 = boundary lubrication (MoP is mainly boundary).
- **Larger heads and greater clearance** influence lubrication; **radial clearance** must be small for MoM fluid-film.
- **Stress shielding** (Wolff's law): bone is resorbed where the stiff implant carries the load: **proximal femoral bone loss** with stiff, large-diameter, extensively coated stems (CoCr more than Ti). Stem stiffness proportional to radius to the 4th power.
- **Cemented stem philosophies:** **taper-slip (force-closed, e.g. Exeter)**: polished, collarless, double-tapered stem **subsides within the cement** (creep) producing hoop stresses and compressive load transfer; **composite-beam (shape-closed, e.g. Charnley-type rough/matt stems)**: stem bonded to cement, no subsidence wanted; **a rough stem debonding generates debris** and fails.
- **Uncemented fixation:** **ingrowth** (porous coating; **pore size about 50-400 micrometres**, ideally 100-400) vs **ongrowth** (grit-blasted, plasma-sprayed). **Micromotion must be under about 40-150 micrometres** for bony ingrowth (over about 150 = fibrous tissue). **Gaps under about 50 micrometres** for ingrowth.

## 9. Ligament and tendon mechanics (brief)
- Load-elongation curve: **toe region** (straightening of crimped collagen), **linear (elastic) region**, yield, failure.
- **Ligaments** contain more elastin and less organised collagen than tendons; viscoelastic; **immobilisation reduces strength and stiffness**; insertion sites recover more slowly than mid-substance.
- **Graft strength (ACL):** native ACL about 2,160 N (Woo); **quadrupled hamstring graft about 4,000 N**; bone-patellar tendon-bone about 2,900 N (10 mm graft); graft is weakest at about 6-12 weeks (necrosis and revascularisation, ligamentisation).

> Exam pearl: **Modulus order: ceramic > CoCr > stainless steel > titanium > cortical bone > PMMA > PE > cancellous bone > tendon > cartilage. Titanium is closest to bone but poor at wear; CoCr is the bearing metal; 316L corrodes most (crevice).** Toughness = area under the curve; most implant failures are fatigue.

> Exam pearl: **Strain under 2% = primary healing (absolute stability); 2-10% = callus; over 10% = non-union.** Nail and pin stiffness vary with radius to the 4th power; plate stiffness with thickness cubed; nail torsional stiffness falls with working length (bending with its square). **Increase pin diameter first** to stiffen an external fixator.

> Exam pearl: **Hip JRF about 3 x BW in single-leg stance; cane in the contralateral hand, load in the ipsilateral hand, medialise the cup, increase offset.** Gamma irradiation in air causes PE oxidation; **remelting removes free radicals but lowers mechanical strength**; annealing keeps strength but leaves radicals. **PMMA: benzoyl peroxide initiates, DMPT accelerates, hydroquinone stabilises**; strongest in compression, a grout not a glue.

nerve and muscle.md:
## 1. Peripheral nerve structure
### The neuron
- **Cell body:** motor neurons in the **anterior horn** of the spinal cord; sensory neurons in the **dorsal root ganglion (DRG)**, outside the cord in the intervertebral foramen; autonomic in sympathetic ganglia.
- **Axon:** carries the action potential; **axonal transport** moves proteins and organelles:
  - **Fast anterograde** (about 100-400 mm/day; **kinesin**, microtubules): vesicles, neurotransmitters.
  - **Slow anterograde** (about 1-6 mm/day): cytoskeletal proteins; sets the **pace of regeneration**.
