  - **Retrograde** (**dynein**): trophic signals (NGF), and route of **tetanus toxin, rabies, herpes, polio** to the cell body.
- **Myelin:** in the **PNS** made by **Schwann cells (one Schwann cell myelinates one internode of one axon)**; in the CNS by **oligodendrocytes** (one cell myelinates many axons). Unmyelinated axons are grouped within a single Schwann cell (Remak bundles).
- **Saltatory conduction:** action potential jumps between **nodes of Ranvier** (voltage-gated sodium channels concentrated at nodes): faster, energy-efficient. **Conduction velocity rises with diameter and myelination.**
- **Resting membrane potential about -70 mV** (Na-K ATPase: 3 Na out, 2 K in; membrane mainly permeable to K). Depolarisation by **Na influx**, repolarisation by **K efflux**.

### Connective tissue layers (very commonly tested)
| Layer | Surrounds | Function / exam point |
|---|---|---|
| **Endoneurium** | **Individual axons** (with their Schwann cells) | Loose collagen; contains endoneurial fluid and capillaries |
| **Perineurium** | **Fascicles** | **Blood-nerve barrier** (tight junctions); main source of **tensile strength** of the nerve; maintains intrafascicular pressure; **cut perineurium = fascicular herniation** |
| **Epineurium** (internal and external) | **Whole nerve** and between fascicles | Cushions fascicles against compression; **sutured in epineurial repair**; most abundant where nerves cross joints |
| **Mesoneurium** | Loose tissue attaching the nerve to surroundings | Carries segmental vessels; allows **nerve gliding** (excursion) |

- **Blood supply:** **extrinsic segmental vessels** (via mesoneurium) and a rich **intrinsic longitudinal plexus** (epineurial, perineurial, endoneurial); allows mobilisation over long segments.
- **Stretch tolerance:** venous flow impaired at about **8% elongation**; **ischaemia at about 15%**; repair under tension fails (limit to minimal tension; graft rather than stretch).
- **Compression:** about **20-30 mmHg** impairs epineurial venular flow and axonal transport; **about 30-40 mmHg** causes paraesthesia and conduction changes; about 50-80 mmHg blocks conduction. Basis of carpal tunnel pathophysiology (normal carpal tunnel pressure about 2-10 mmHg; raised in wrist flexion and extension).

### Fibre classification
| Fibre (Erlanger-Gasser) | Lloyd (sensory) | Myelin | Velocity | Function |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A-alpha** | **Ia, Ib** | Thick | Fastest (about 70-120 m/s) | **Alpha motor neurons**; **muscle spindle primary afferent (Ia)**, **Golgi tendon organ (Ib)** |
| **A-beta** | II | Yes | 30-70 m/s | Touch, pressure, vibration, spindle secondary |
| **A-gamma** | | Yes | 15-30 m/s | **Motor to muscle spindle** (intrafusal fibres) |
| **A-delta** | III | Thin | 5-30 m/s | **Fast (sharp) pain, cold** |
| **B** | | Thin | 3-15 m/s | Preganglionic autonomic |
| **C** | IV | **Unmyelinated** | **Slowest (under 2 m/s)** | **Slow (burning) pain, warmth, postganglionic sympathetic** |

- **Local anaesthetics block small fibres first:** **B (autonomic) > A-delta and C (pain, temperature) > A-beta (touch, pressure) > A-alpha (motor, proprioception)**; clinically sympathetic block, then pain, temperature, touch, motor; recovery is in the reverse order. Pressure (tourniquet) blocks large fibres first.

### Sensory receptors
| Receptor | Adaptation | Modality |
|---|---|---|
| **Meissner corpuscle** | Rapid | **Light moving touch**, **moving two-point discrimination** (glabrous skin) |
| **Pacinian corpuscle** | Rapid | **Vibration, deep pressure** |
| **Merkel disc** | Slow | **Static touch and pressure**, **static two-point discrimination** |
| **Ruffini ending** | Slow | **Skin stretch**, joint position |
| Free nerve endings | Slow | Pain, temperature |
| **Muscle spindle** | | Muscle **length** and rate of change (stretch reflex) |
| **Golgi tendon organ** | | Muscle **tension** (inhibits contraction: autogenic inhibition) |

- **Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments** (threshold test, slowly adapting fibres) are the **most sensitive test in early compression neuropathy**; **two-point discrimination** (innervation density test) becomes abnormal later, with axonal loss; **normal static 2PD at fingertip under about 6 mm**.
- **Vibration (256 Hz tuning fork)** is also an early threshold test.

## 2. Nerve injury classification
| Seddon | Sunderland | Pathology | Tinel sign | Recovery | Management |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Neurapraxia** | **I** | **Focal demyelination / conduction block**; axon intact; **no Wallerian degeneration** | Not advancing | **Complete, within days to about 12 weeks**; motor often more affected than sensory | Observe |
| **Axonotmesis** | **II** | **Axon disrupted**, endoneurium intact | **Advances** about 1 mm/day | **Complete** (tubes guide axons to correct targets) | Observe |
| | **III** | Axon and **endoneurium** disrupted; perineurium intact | Advances | **Incomplete, variable** (misdirection, intrafascicular scarring) | Observe; surgery if no recovery |
| | **IV** | Only **epineurium** intact (**neuroma-in-continuity**) | Does not advance | **None useful** | **Excision of neuroma and repair/graft** |
| **Neurotmesis** | **V** | **Complete transection** | No advance | **None** | **Surgical repair** |
| | **VI (Mackinnon)** | **Mixed** injury: different fascicles have different degrees | Variable | Variable | Intraoperative stimulation; repair only non-functioning parts |

- **Clinical rule:** an **advancing Tinel sign** indicates regenerating axons (degree II-III); a static Tinel at the injury suggests neuroma (IV-V).
- **Sharp open injury with deficit** = assume transection: explore. **Closed or blunt injury** = most are neurapraxia or axonotmesis: observe.

## 3. Degeneration and regeneration
### After axonal injury
1. **Wallerian degeneration** of the **distal segment** (begins within hours to days; axon and myelin fragment). Distal nerve **remains excitable for about 3-7 days** (useful for intraoperative stimulation of the distal stump in the first days).
2. **Schwann cells** proliferate, help **macrophages** clear debris, and line up in tubes (**bands of Büngner**), producing **neurotrophic factors (NGF, BDNF, GDNF)**.
3. **Proximal segment:** degenerates back for one or a few nodes (more if injury is close to the cell body: **retrograde degeneration, cell death in proximal injuries**).
4. **Cell body:** **chromatolysis** (Nissl substance disperses, nucleus moves to the periphery, cell swells), switching to production of structural proteins.
5. **Regeneration:** the proximal axon sprouts a **growth cone** (multiple sprouts), guided by:
   - **Neurotropism:** growth **towards** the distal stump (target-directed, chemotactic).
   - **Neurotrophism:** factors that **support survival and growth** (NGF, etc.).
   - **Contact guidance** along basal lamina tubes.
6. **Rate:** about **1 mm/day (about 1 inch per month)**, after an initial delay of a few weeks crossing the repair site; slower in older patients and more distally.
- **Motor end-plates and muscle:** after denervation, muscle atrophies; **motor end-plates degenerate and muscle becomes fibrotic**: **reinnervation must reach the muscle within about 12-18 months** (often taught 12-18 months; fibrosis irreversible by about 18-24 months). **Sensory receptors tolerate denervation longer**: protective sensation can still be regained after years.
- Hence **distance from injury to target** determines whether nerve repair can work: a proximal (high) injury with distance over about 18 inches (45 cm) to target may never reinnerve intrinsic muscles: **nerve transfer or tendon transfer** instead.

### Factors affecting outcome of repair
- **Age** (single most important; **children recover best**).
- **Level** (distal better than proximal), **delay** to repair, **gap / tension**, **mechanism** (sharp better than crush, avulsion or blast), associated vascular and soft-tissue injury.
- **Type of nerve:** pure motor or pure sensory better than mixed; typical order of recovery: **radial > musculocutaneous > median > ulnar**; **peroneal (common fibular) has the worst prognosis** of the lower limb (tibial recovers better).

## 4. Electrodiagnosis
### Nerve conduction studies (NCS)
- **Latency** (time to response), **amplitude** (number of functioning axons), **conduction velocity** (myelin).
- **Demyelination:** **prolonged latency, slowed velocity**, conduction block; amplitude relatively preserved.
- **Axonal loss:** **reduced amplitude** (CMAP motor, SNAP sensory); velocity near normal.
- **Normal upper limb motor conduction velocity over about 50 m/s**; carpal tunnel: **distal motor latency over about 4.2-4.5 ms** and **sensory latency over about 3.5 ms** abnormal (lab-dependent).
- **Preganglionic (root avulsion) vs postganglionic brachial plexus injury:**
  - In **preganglionic** injury the **DRG and sensory cell body are intact** and connected to the distal axon: **SNAP is PRESERVED** in an anaesthetic limb (**key exam fact**); motor CMAP absent.
  - **Postganglionic:** SNAP and CMAP both lost.
  - Other features of **avulsion**: **Horner syndrome** (C8-T1, sympathetic chain), **winged scapula** (long thoracic nerve) or **rhomboid paralysis** (dorsal scapular), **elevated hemidiaphragm** (phrenic), **pseudomeningocele** on **CT myelogram or MRI**, severe burning pain, **positive histamine test** (intact axon flare). These cannot be repaired directly: **nerve transfers**.
  - **Proximal muscles (rhomboids, serratus, paraspinals) denervated** on EMG imply preganglionic injury.

### Electromyography (EMG)
- **Normal resting muscle:** electrically silent (after insertional activity).
- **Denervation:** **fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves** at rest appear **about 2-3 weeks (10-21 days) after injury** (earlier in proximal muscles, later distally): **wait about 3-4 weeks after injury before EMG** to distinguish neurapraxia from axonal injury.
- **Neurapraxia:** no fibrillations; conduction block across the lesion with **normal conduction distal to it** (even after weeks).
- **Reinnervation:** **nascent (small, polyphasic) motor unit potentials** appear before clinical recovery (often weeks to months earlier): the **earliest sign of recovery**; later large, long-duration polyphasic potentials.
- **Myopathy:** **small, short-duration, polyphasic** motor units with **early recruitment**; neuropathy: **large, long-duration** units with **reduced recruitment**.

## 5. Nerve repair techniques
### Timing
| Situation | Timing |
|---|---|
| **Sharp, clean laceration** | **Primary repair** (within about 72 hours to 1 week; ideally early) |
| **Contused, crushed, contaminated wound** | **Tag ends**, delayed (secondary) repair at about **2-3 weeks** when the zone of injury is demarcated, usually with **graft** |
| **Closed injury / closed fracture with palsy** | **Observe**; EMG at 3-4 weeks and repeat; **explore at about 3-6 months** if no clinical or EMG recovery |
| **Gunshot (low-velocity)** | Usually neurapraxia/axonotmesis: observe |
| **Iatrogenic palsy after a procedure** | If the nerve was at risk and the palsy is complete and immediate, early exploration is often recommended |

- **Radial nerve palsy with humeral shaft fracture** (about 10-12%): **observe**, about **70-90% recover**; explore if **open fracture**, no recovery by about 3-6 months (EMG), or (debated) palsy after closed reduction; **Holstein-Lewis** distal-third spiral fracture classically entraps the nerve.

### Technique
- **Tension-free** repair (joint positioning acceptable within limits), **9-0 or 10-0 nylon**, microscope magnification, align fascicles using **surface vessels (vasa nervorum)** and fascicular pattern.
- **Epineurial repair** (most common) vs **group fascicular (perineurial)** repair: **no proven superiority** of fascicular repair in mixed nerves; fascicular when distinct motor and sensory groups exist (e.g. ulnar nerve at wrist, separating the deep motor branch).
- **Fibrin glue** is an acceptable adjunct.
- **Nerve gaps:**
  - **Autograft = gold standard**: **sural nerve** most common (up to about 30-40 cm, sensory loss over lateral foot); also medial and lateral antebrachial cutaneous, superficial radial, posterior interosseous (terminal, at wrist). Graft is reversed (to avoid axon loss through branches). **Cable grafts** for large nerves.
  - **Hollow conduits** (collagen, PGA, vein): **short gaps (under about 3 cm) in small-diameter sensory nerves** (digital nerves); best under about 1-2 cm.
  - **Processed nerve allograft** (decellularised): sensory gaps up to about 3 cm (data growing for longer and mixed nerves).
- **Nerve transfers** (proximal injuries, avulsions, long distance to target): use a **redundant, expendable motor fascicle close to the target muscle**.

| Transfer | Donor | Recipient | Goal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oberlin** | **Ulnar nerve fascicle** (to FCU) | **Musculocutaneous branch to biceps** | Elbow flexion |
| **Double fascicular (Mackinnon)** | Ulnar FCU fascicle + median FDS/FCR fascicle | Biceps and brachialis branches | Elbow flexion |
| **Spinal accessory to suprascapular** | Distal CN XI (preserve upper trapezius branches) | Suprascapular | Shoulder abduction and external rotation |
| **Leechavengvongs (Somsak)** | Radial branch to **long (or medial) head of triceps** | **Anterior branch of axillary nerve** | Deltoid / shoulder abduction |
| **AIN to ulnar motor** (supercharged end-to-side) | **Anterior interosseous (pronator quadratus branch)** | Deep motor branch of ulnar | Intrinsic function in high ulnar injury |
| Intercostal nerves | Intercostals | Musculocutaneous, etc. | Pan-plexus avulsion |
| Contralateral C7 | Contralateral C7 | Median nerve, etc. | Global avulsion |

- **Tendon transfers:** principles (**donor expendable, adequate strength (loses about one MRC grade after transfer), adequate excursion, straight line of pull, one function per transfer, synergistic, supple joints, tissue equilibrium**); classic radial palsy transfer: **pronator teres to ECRB, FCR or FCU to EDC, palmaris longus to EPL**.

### Neuroma and pain
- **Neuroma:** disorganised axonal sprouting at a nerve end or in continuity; painful neuromas treated by excision and burial in muscle/bone, **targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)** or regenerative peripheral nerve interface (RPNI).
- **Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS):** type I (no identifiable nerve injury), type II (with nerve injury; causalgia); **Budapest criteria**; **vitamin C (500 mg daily for 50 days)** reduces CRPS after distal radius fractures (Zollinger; supported in AAOS distal radius guidance, though the evidence is debated).

## 6. Skeletal muscle structure
- **Connective tissue:** **epimysium** (whole muscle), **perimysium** (fascicles), **endomysium** (individual fibres).
- **Muscle fibre** (cell): multinucleated syncytium; **sarcolemma**, **T-tubules** (invaginations carrying depolarisation), **sarcoplasmic reticulum** (stores calcium; terminal cisternae either side of a T-tubule = **triad**).
- **Myofibrils** made of repeating **sarcomeres** (functional contractile unit, **Z line to Z line**).

### The sarcomere
| Band | Content | Change on contraction |
|---|---|---|
| **A band** | **Full length of myosin (thick) filaments**, with overlapping actin | **Constant length** |
| **I band** | **Actin (thin) filaments only**; Z line in the middle | **Shortens** |
| **H zone** | **Myosin only** (no overlap) | **Shortens / disappears** |
| **M line** | Centre of the A band; links myosin | Constant |
| **Z line (disc)** | Anchors actin (alpha-actinin) | Lines move closer |

- Remember: **"A" band is Always the same; H and I shorten** (sliding filament theory: filaments slide, they do not shorten).
- **Thin filament:** **actin**, **tropomyosin** (covers myosin-binding sites at rest), **troponin complex: troponin C (binds calcium), troponin I (inhibits actin-myosin interaction), troponin T (binds tropomyosin)**.
- **Thick filament:** **myosin** (heads with ATPase activity).
- **Titin:** giant elastic protein from Z line to M line (passive tension); **nebulin** on actin; **dystrophin** links the cytoskeleton (actin) to the sarcolemma and extracellular matrix through the dystroglycan complex (absent in **Duchenne**, reduced/abnormal in **Becker**).

### Excitation-contraction coupling
1. Motor neuron action potential reaches the **neuromuscular junction**; **calcium influx** (voltage-gated Ca channels) triggers release of **acetylcholine (ACh)**.
2. ACh binds **nicotinic receptors** on the motor end-plate: sodium influx, **end-plate potential**, muscle action potential.
3. ACh is broken down by **acetylcholinesterase**.
4. Action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down **T-tubules**; the **dihydropyridine receptor (voltage sensor)** mechanically opens the **ryanodine receptor (RyR1)** on the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
5. **Calcium released** binds **troponin C**; tropomyosin moves, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin.
6. **Cross-bridge cycling:** myosin head binds actin, power stroke (release of ADP and Pi), **ATP binding detaches the head** (no ATP = **rigor mortis**), ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head.
7. **Relaxation:** calcium pumped back into the SR by **SERCA (Ca-ATPase, needs ATP)**.

### Applied pharmacology and pathology of the NMJ and coupling
| Condition / drug | Site | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Myasthenia gravis** | **Antibodies to postsynaptic nicotinic AChR** | Fatigable weakness; improves with anticholinesterases (edrophonium/neostigmine) |
| **Lambert-Eaton syndrome** | **Antibodies to presynaptic voltage-gated Ca channels** (small cell lung cancer) | Weakness improving with repeated use |
| **Botulinum toxin** | **Blocks presynaptic ACh release** (cleaves SNARE proteins) | Flaccid paralysis; therapeutic in **spasticity (cerebral palsy)**; effect about 3-6 months (sprouting) |
| **Non-depolarising relaxants** (rocuronium, vecuronium) | **Competitive AChR antagonists** | Reversed by neostigmine or sugammadex (rocuronium) |
| **Succinylcholine** | **Depolarising** agonist | Fasciculation then paralysis; **hyperkalaemia** in burns, denervation, spinal cord injury, **Duchenne** and other myopathies (avoid) |
| **Organophosphates** | Inhibit acetylcholinesterase | Cholinergic crisis |
| **Malignant hyperthermia** | **RYR1 mutation** (autosomal dominant; also CACNA1S) | Uncontrolled SR calcium release with **volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine**: rising end-tidal CO2 (earliest sign), tachycardia, rigidity, hyperthermia (late), rhabdomyolysis; treat with **dantrolene** (blocks RyR1), stop triggers, cool. Linked with **central core disease** and King-Denborough syndrome; hyperthermia under anaesthesia is also reported in **osteogenesis imperfecta and arthrogryposis** (usually not true MH) |

## 7. Muscle fibre types and motor units
| Property | **Type I (slow oxidative)** | **Type IIA (fast oxidative-glycolytic)** | **Type IIB/IIX (fast glycolytic)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colour | **Red** (myoglobin) | Red-pink | **White** |
| Contraction speed | **Slow** | Fast | **Fastest** |
| Force | **Low** | Intermediate | **High** |
| Metabolism | **Aerobic (oxidative)**: many mitochondria, capillaries | Both | **Anaerobic glycolysis**: glycogen-rich |
| Fatigue | **Resistant** | Intermediate | **Rapid** |
| Motor unit size | Small | Intermediate | **Large** |
| Typical use | **Posture, endurance** (soleus, paraspinals) | Middle distance | **Sprint, power** |

- **Mnemonic: "one slow fat red ox"**: type 1, slow, red, oxidative.
- **Motor unit:** one motor neuron and all the fibres it supplies (all of the same fibre type). **Small motor units** (few fibres) in muscles needing **fine control** (extraocular, intrinsic hand); large units in gastrocnemius, quadriceps.
- **Henneman size principle:** **small motor units (type I) are recruited first**, larger (type II) units as force increases.
- **Training:**
  - **Endurance training:** increases **mitochondria, capillary density, oxidative enzymes, myoglobin**; fibre-type shift towards oxidative (IIX to IIA).
  - **Strength training:** early gains are **neural** (recruitment, synchronisation); later **hypertrophy** (increased cross-sectional area of fibres, mainly type II); hyperplasia is minimal in humans.
- **Muscle force is proportional to physiological cross-sectional area**; **velocity and excursion are proportional to fibre length**. Pennate muscles (quadriceps, gastrocnemius) produce high force; long parallel-fibred muscles (sartorius) produce excursion.
- **Ageing (sarcopenia):** loss of fibres and **preferential atrophy of type II fibres**.
- **Disuse / immobilisation:** rapid atrophy (begins within days), **type I fibres are affected early** (antigravity muscles like quadriceps and soleus most affected); **immobilising in a lengthened position reduces atrophy**. **Corticosteroid myopathy** affects type II fibres.

### Types of contraction
| Type | Definition | Example / point |
|---|---|---|
| **Isometric** | Tension without change in length | Static holding; early rehabilitation |
| **Isotonic** | **Constant load (tension)** through the range; velocity varies | Free weights |
| **Concentric** | Muscle **shortens** while contracting | Lifting phase |
| **Eccentric** | Muscle **lengthens** while contracting | **Generates the greatest force**, most metabolically efficient, **most likely to cause strain and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)**; used therapeutically in tendinopathy (Alfredson heel drops) |
| **Isokinetic** | **Constant velocity** with variable resistance (machine) | Best for strength **testing and rehabilitation**, maximises force throughout the range |
| **Plyometric** | Rapid eccentric followed by concentric (stretch-shortening cycle) | Jump training; power |
| Closed kinetic chain | Distal segment fixed | Squats: less ACL graft strain, better co-contraction early after ACL reconstruction |

- **Length-tension relationship:** maximal active force at **resting length** (optimal actin-myosin overlap); less at shortened or overstretched lengths. Total tension at long lengths includes passive (titin, connective tissue) tension.
- **Force-velocity relationship:** concentric force falls as velocity rises; **eccentric force exceeds isometric**.

### Energy systems
| System | Duration | Fuel / by-product |
|---|---|---|
| **ATP-creatine phosphate (phosphagen)** | **First about 10-15 s** (e.g. 100 m sprint, lifting) | No oxygen; no lactate |
| **Anaerobic glycolysis (lactic acid system)** | **About 15 s to 2 min** (400 m) | Glycogen to **lactate** (fatigue, acidosis) |
| **Aerobic (oxidative)** | **Beyond about 2 min** (endurance) | Glucose, fatty acids via Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; most ATP |
- **Creatine supplementation** increases phosphocreatine stores (short, repeated high-intensity effort).

## 8. Muscle injury, healing and disorders
### Muscle strain
- Occurs at the **myotendinous junction** (commonest site) during **eccentric contraction**.
- At risk: **muscles crossing two joints** with a high proportion of **type II fibres**: **hamstrings (biceps femoris long head commonest)**, **rectus femoris**, **medial head of gastrocnemius** ("tennis leg"), adductor longus.
- Healing phases: **destruction** (necrosis, haematoma, inflammation), **repair** (phagocytosis, **satellite cell** activation and regeneration of myofibres, scar formation), **remodelling**. Scar tissue competes with regeneration.
- **Short immobilisation (a few days) then early controlled mobilisation** gives the best healing (regeneration aligned, less scar).
- **Proximal hamstring avulsion:** surgical repair if **two or more tendons are avulsed with over about 2 cm retraction** (commonly quoted) or in high-demand patients; early repair (within about 4-6 weeks) gives better results.

### Contusion and myositis ossificans
- Direct blow (quadriceps commonest): haematoma; **immobilise the knee in about 120 degrees of flexion for the first 24 hours** after quadriceps contusion (reduces stiffness and time to return).
- **Myositis ossificans (heterotopic ossification after trauma):** mass within weeks; **zonal pattern** with **mature ossification at the periphery and immature centre** (the opposite of **parosteal/surface osteosarcoma**, which is most mature centrally); separated from cortex by a lucent cleft. Excise only when **mature** (about 6-12 months; bone scan cold, well-corticated) if symptomatic.

### Denervation and other effects on muscle
- **Denervation:** atrophy, **fibrillations** on EMG (2-3 weeks), progressive fibrosis; irreversible end-plate loss after about 12-18 months (see above).
- **Compartment syndrome:** muscle ischaemia causes irreversible necrosis after about **4-6 hours** (commonly quoted 6 hours); **delta pressure (diastolic BP minus compartment pressure) under 30 mmHg** = fasciotomy (McQueen); absolute pressure over 30 mmHg in some protocols. Late result **Volkmann ischaemic contracture** (deep flexor compartment of forearm: FDP and FPL most affected).
- **Rhabdomyolysis:** myoglobinuria, very high CK, hyperkalaemia; risk of **acute kidney injury**; aggressive IV fluids.
- **Tourniquet:** muscle more sensitive than nerve to ischaemia in the long run; **nerve injury under the cuff is mainly mechanical (pressure)**; limit about **2 hours** upper and lower limb (commonly quoted), pressure about 50-75 mmHg above systolic for arm and about 100-150 mmHg above systolic for thigh (or limb occlusion pressure based).

### Muscle disorders seen in orthopaedics
| Disorder | Key features |
|---|---|
| **Duchenne muscular dystrophy** | **X-linked recessive**, **dystrophin absent (Xp21)**; boys, onset about 3-5 years, **Gowers sign**, **calf pseudohypertrophy** (fat and fibrous replacement), **CK markedly raised (10-100 x)**; loss of ambulation about 10-12 years (later with steroids); scoliosis (fuse early when curve over about 20-30 degrees and FVC adequate, over about 30-35% predicted); cardiomyopathy; avoid succinylcholine and volatile agents (hyperkalaemic rhabdomyolysis) |
| **Becker muscular dystrophy** | X-linked, **reduced/abnormal dystrophin**, milder, later onset, walks beyond about 15 years |
| **Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy** | **Autosomal dominant**, face and **scapular winging**; scapulothoracic fusion improves shoulder elevation |
| **Myotonic dystrophy** | Autosomal dominant, **CTG repeat (DMPK)**, myotonia, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, anticipation |
| **Spinal muscular atrophy** | **Anterior horn cell** loss, **SMN1** deletion (autosomal recessive); proximal weakness, no sensory loss; **nusinersen**, onasemnogene; scoliosis |
| **Polymyositis / dermatomyositis** | Inflammatory, proximal weakness, raised CK, MRI-guided biopsy |

> Exam pearl: **Perineurium = blood-nerve barrier and tensile strength; epineurium is sutured; endoneurium surrounds single axons.** Sunderland I = neurapraxia, II-IV = axonotmesis grades, V = neurotmesis, VI = mixed (Mackinnon). Regeneration about **1 mm/day**; motor end-plates must be reached within about **12-18 months**.

> Exam pearl: **Fibrillations appear about 2-3 weeks after denervation: do EMG at 3-4 weeks. Nascent polyphasic units = earliest sign of reinnervation. Preserved SNAP in an anaesthetic limb = preganglionic (root avulsion) injury.** Sural nerve is the commonest graft; conduits only for short (under about 3 cm) sensory gaps. Oberlin = ulnar fascicle to biceps branch.

> Exam pearl: **A band constant; H zone and I band shorten. Calcium binds troponin C; ATP detaches myosin (rigor without ATP). RYR1 = malignant hyperthermia (dantrolene).** Type I = slow, red, oxidative, small units recruited first (Henneman). **Eccentric contraction = greatest force and most strains**; strains occur at the myotendinous junction of two-joint muscles. Myositis ossificans matures at the periphery.
